news.title: Taylor Swift Reportedly 'Takes Action' Over a Donald Trump Post Bragging About Zero 'Illegals'
news.text: Taylor Swift's 'Father Figure' was no longer audible on a Team Trump Instagram post by Thursday, 24 September 2026, after the account used the track on a political graphic featuring President Donald Trump.The post was shared on 23 September and claimed that US border crossings had increased. The @TeamTrump post used artwork styled around Swift's 'Patient Zero' rollout and claimed that 'Zer(illegals) have crossed our borders in 16+ months.'It initially carried 'Father Figure' as its soundtrack. By the following day, the post displayed the message, 'This sound isn't available.'The border wording needs qualification. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) data show Southwest Border Patrol recorded 6,068 apprehensions in June 2025, 4,596 in July and 6,321 in August. Those totals were low by recent standards, but they were not zero.The Trump administration has made a separate claim about releases after apprehension. On 9 September 2026, the White House said Border Patrol had released no 'illegal alien' into the country for 15 straight months. CBP later announced 16 consecutive months of zero releases. That is not the same measure as crossings or apprehensions.Taylor Swift Audio Removal Remains UnconfirmedThe missing audio quickly prompted speculation that Swift or her representatives had intervened. Available reports, however, cite no confirmation from Swift, Team Trump, Instagram or Meta explaining who removed the track or why.That distinction is crucial. The confirmed development is simply that 'Father Figure' initially accompanied the post and later became unavailable. Saying Swift 'took action' would assign a cause that has not been established.There is relevant history. In August 2026, Reuters reported that Swift songs had disappeared from several social media posts published by the White House and Trump's campaign. One Team Trump TikTok had used 'August' over footage of Donald and Melania Trump watching fireworks.Reuters said neither the White House nor a Swift representative immediately responded to requests for comment about those removals. Swift had not publicly explained them.The political history between Swift and Trump is clearer. Swift endorsed Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election after supporting Joe Biden in 2020. Five days after her Harris endorsement, Trump posted 'I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!' on Truth Social on 15 September 2024.He referred to her again in May 2025, writing, 'Has anyone noticed that, since I said 'I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,' she's no longer 'HOT?'' Those exchanges help explain the attention around another Trump-linked post using her music. They do not show what happened behind the scenes this time.Other Artists Have Objected To Trump-Linked Music UseOther musicians have made direct, public objections when their songs appeared in Trump administration or campaign material.In December 2025, the White House used Sabrina Carpenter's 'Juno' in a social media video showing immigration enforcement arrests. Carpenter responded, 'This video is evil and disgusting. Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.'Ariana Grande objected in June 2026 after the White House used 'Bye' in a TikTok video showing federal immigration enforcement activity. She wrote, 'Please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense.'Reuters reported that a source close to Grande said her team was looking into removing the song. White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson defended the video, saying, 'what's actually barbaric, inhumane, and heinous are the criminal illegal aliens who have injured and murdered innocent American citizens.'Earlier disputes involved other artists. ABBA asked Trump's campaign in 2024 to stop using its music at rallies, with Universal Music saying no permission or licence had been granted. Céline Dion's representatives separately described the campaign's use of one of her performances as unauthorised.In Swift's latest case, the Team Trump post remained accessible after 'Father Figure' disappeared. No public explanation from Swift, her representatives, Team Trump or Instagram had established who caused the audio change.

news.title: Bring On The Generals: Roughly 60% Of Polled Democrats Would Support A Military Coup
news.text:
Authored by Jonathan Turley via JonathanTurley.org,

It is the same "nostalgia" that leaves many of us shocked at the support for a military coup. 

On our 250th anniversary, we face yet again Benjamin Franklin's warning that this is a Republic if we can keep it.

news.title: The Patriot Post® · Toward a Post-Trump Politics
news.text:
From the clutter of midterm election poll results, it’s possible sometimes to see new patterns of political support emerging.

The overall pattern, as it stands, makes some sense. As in the 2006 and 2018 off-year cycles, the Republican president’s job approval had sagged to well below 50%. Polls at this point in the year showed Democrats competitive in states and districts that the president had carried by solid margins two years before.

Democrats ended up gaining 30 House seats in 2006 and 41 in 2018, ousting Republican speakers and, in both elections, installing Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.). A similar result is expected this time, with Democrats needing to gain only three seats to win control, though Pelosi is retiring from Congress at age 86.

Such gains are not necessarily inevitable. Census redistricting ended up favoring Republicans. As Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini has pointed out, the summer polling understated Republicans’ fall polling and November percentages in Senate races in 2014, 2018 and 2022. But he spots no similar move in polls conducted up through mid-September.

What I find striking is a sharp divergence in Senate polling between what have turned out to be seriously contested races in the North and in the South.

According to RealClearPolitics, in the South, Democrats have big leads in North Carolina (+8) and Georgia (+7). They narrowly lead in Texas (+2) and are only slightly behind in South Carolina (-3). In each state, they’re polling far ahead of Trump 2024 benchmarks in North Carolina (Trump +3), Georgia (Trump +2), Texas (Trump +14) and South Carolina (Trump +18).

Overall, these Trump +9 Southern states are averaging +3 Democratic in Senate races — a big +12 Democratic swing.

The picture is different in four states up on the Canadian border. Democrats have only narrow edges in RealClearPolitics averages in Maine (+2), New Hampshire (+5), Michigan (+3) and Minnesota (+4). These numbers are in line with 2024 benchmarks in Maine (Harris +7), New Hampshire (Harris +3), Michigan (Trump +1) and Minnesota (Harris +4).

Overall, these four states that averaged Harris +3 are now averaging Democrats +3. No swing at all.

What accounts for the difference? One answer that quickly occurs is candidate selection.

Trump effectively chose the Republican nominees in the Southern races. He prompted the retirement of the occasionally anti-Trump incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and replaced him with the unknown Michael Whatley to run against a reputedly centrist two-term Democratic governor.

He issued a late endorsement of scandal-prone state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Texas Republican runoff rather than incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and evidently never considered the young Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-Texas), who ran third in the primary.

After the sudden death of incumbent South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham in July, Trump encouraged his inexperienced sister Darline Graham Nordone to run for the remainder of his term and endorsed her to run in November for a full term.

And while contesting the 2020 result in Georgia, Trump discouraged Republican turnout in the two January 2021 runoffs, which enabled Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) and Rafael Warnock (D-Ga.) to win 51% to 49%. Warnock won a full term against Trump-endorsed Herschel Walker by the same margin in 2022, and Ossoff seems headed for a bigger win this year. That gives the two Democrats 20 years in the Senate from a state that didn’t elect a Democratic senator between 2000 and 2021.

Meanwhile, up by the Canadian border, left-wing and anti-Israel Democratic activists and primary voters have given their party’s Senate nominations to candidates who, so far at least, are running behind former Vice President Kamala Harris’s percentages in their states.

Running closest to Harris is Democratic Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who led primary polls by wide margins but won the primary by only 48.4% to 47.6%. A charismatic campaigner, he may have been hurt by bringing into his campaign the streamer Hasan Piker, who famously declared that America “deserved 9/11,” and by responding to an attack on a synagogue in March by saying, “Hurt people hurt people.”

Running further behind Harris is Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, winner of the Democratic-Farmer-Labor party nomination, who, as lieutenant governor, has been attacked for failure to prevent the hundreds of millions of dollars of Medicaid fraud by Somali immigrants.

The national spotlight has not been kind to Gov. Tim Walz (D-Minn.) since he was selected by Harris for the vice presidential nomination — his weak debate performance and the fraud perpetrated against his administration tarnished his party in a state whose many Scandinavian- and German-descended voters have been proud of the state’s and the DFL’s reputation for probity and competence.

Local and personal factors help explain Democrats’ apparent difficulty in nailing down Senate wins in northern New England. In New Hampshire, John Sununu, son and brother of governors, won the same Senate seat in 2002 and lost it in 2008. The centrist record of his brother Chris Sununu, governor from 2017 to 2025, has made him surprisingly competitive in a high-education, Trump-averse state, which national Democrats have deprived of its first-in-the-nation presidential primary.

In Maine, Republican Susan Collins, after 30 years in the Senate, chairs the Appropriations Committee and has a moderate record, which helped her win reelection in 2020 by 51% to 42% after Democrat Sara Gideon outspent her two-to-one and led in every public poll.

This year, Democrats nominated Graham Platner, Marine veteran and oysterman, though he turned out to have a Nazi tattoo, and his only oyster customer was his mother’s restaurant. Forced out by allegations of sexual harassment, he was replaced in September by logger Troy Jackson, whose working-class credentials seemed stronger but who had finished only third, with 21%, in the June primary for governor.

All of which looks like the beginning — the birthing pains, you might say — of a post-Donald Trump politics. The Republican polling firm Echelon Insights has been asking respondents whether they are “Trump-first” or “party-first” Republicans. In February 2025, a month after Trump’s second inauguration and two months before his “liberation day” tariffs, Trump-first Republicans outnumbered party-firsters by a record 63% to 33%.

That was bound to decline at some point, and it has. This September, party-first Republicans, at 56%, significantly outnumbered Trump-first Republicans at 34%.

That inevitable process may have been sped up by Trump’s stubborn preoccupation with issues of personal importance to him — putting his name on the Kennedy Center or demolishing it, the ballroom and triumphal arch, cryptocurrency — but of no value to the party or its voters, current and potential.

If I were a Democratic candidate, I’d consider plagiarizing the effective 2024 pro-Trump ad “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you” with “Donald Trump is for him/his, this Democrat is for you.”

In the meantime, Republicans, at least in the four northern Senate races mentioned here, seem to be getting in the habit of nominating candidates suited to local terrain and emphasizing issues tailored to their states — NFL commentator Michele Tafoya in Minnesota, seven-term congressman from a marginal district Mike Rogers in Michigan, and John Sununu in New Hampshire.

Gambling on many such candidates, as Democrat Rahm Emanuel did while heading his party’s House campaign committee in the 2006 cycle, can be an effective way of expanding one’s party to new constituencies.

In contrast, the Democratic Party today is saddled with a dominant faction, white college graduates, that demands obeisance to defense of wildly unpopular stands on cultural issues, from defunding the police to open-borders immigration to boys in girls’ sports. Some even insist on sympathizing with the motives of those who launch armed attacks on synagogues.

Americans in the 21st century have, in increasing numbers, voted straight party tickets for or against candidates backing policies associated with George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Trump. How that works out depends on decisions not yet made and events that have not yet occurred.

Poll numbers have Democrats favored to win majorities in the House of Representatives and, by narrower margins, the Senate. But disparate regional trends suggest the Republicans may be getting a head start at what my Washington Examiner colleague Byron York calls “moving into the pro-Trump future.”

news.title: The Patriot Post® · Toxic Kamala Hits the Campaign Trail
news.text:
Of all the advantages President Donald Trump has enjoyed in his three presidential campaigns, none has been as great as the considerably low quality of his competition. Since Barack Obama left office, the Democratic Party has trotted out Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden, and Kamala Harris as nominees.

It’s almost certain that Clinton would have lost to any candidate the GOP threw at her, and 2020 was a perfect storm of the Democrat Party and national media operating at unprecedented levels in throwing their weight behind their candidate, paired with Trump’s COVID albatross.

In 2024, Trump returned to face Kamala Harris. It quickly became evident that Harris was out of her depth in anything related to campaigning. Her ability to answer questions like a seven-year-old was staggering, and voters saw President Trump, enjoying a rare surge of positive publicity, as the more electable candidate.

Fast-forward two years later, and somehow Harris is still a major figure in the Democrat Party. Not only that, but she’s in contention for the Democrat nomination in 2028. Will she win the nomination? My guess is no, but by default, she will still have a fighting chance.

Harris may be gearing up for a third attempt at the presidency. She is hitting the campaign trail and has found a home with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

Why did I use the words “found a home”?

In short, most Democrat nominees don’t want to be associated with her in any way, and I don’t blame them. Iowa gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand gave Harris a simple “No thanks,” while Kansas Senate nominee Adam Hamilton is aiming for voters whose “worldview may be a bit different than Kamala Harris.” She has seen similar rejections in Texas and Arizona. Even in her home state of California, only 28% of voters are excited for a Harris 2028 run.

Abdul El-Sayed might be one of the few candidates who could reasonably justify bringing someone along like Harris. He’s such an extreme leftist on his own that Harris wouldn’t be unpalatable for his supporters, and he particularly lacks black support in the tight Michigan race. On paper, Harris, who is famous for changing her accent around different ethnicities, should be able to help with that.

El-Sayed might be a little disappointed in that regard.

At a campaign event featuring Harris and El-Sayed, it was clear that the former vice president hasn’t improved on her public speaking abilities one bit. El-Sayed looked like he was in visible pain as Harris rambled about black maternal healthcare. Even he, who is seen by many as a glorified activist with little experience in the political world, can see how poor a politician Harris really is. Democrat leaders don’t like her for a reason, and Abdul El-Sayed learned it the hard way.

Kamala Harris may help Abdul El-Sayed make small gains in Michigan, but she’s more likely to alienate the voters El-Sayed needs on his side. That simply reflects the former veep’s campaign abilities.

It is certainly possible to cultivate political skills regardless of your platform. Zohran Mamdani, for example, has a horrible platform but good political chops. Kamala Harris has had the opposite effect. She has spent her career leaching off of more capable people. On her own, she has been the Democrats’ ball and chain that has dragged the party down.

Looking ahead to this midterm and the presidential election to follow, I can only hope that Harris throws everything she has toward these midterm campaigns and then eventually, toward her own campaign in two years. In this age, where the GOP’s chances for the next election cycle aren’t looking so bright, it might require one more poor Democrat candidate like Kamala Harris to give the Republicans the victory.

news.title: Kamala Harris Is Quietly Reaching Out to the Voters She Thought She Didn’t Need in 2024. They’re Listening—Carefully.
news.text:
As the national political environment for Democrats shifts rapidly, Kamala Harris is teasing another run for president. At Al Sharpton’s National Action Network convention, when a crowd began chanting “Run again!,” Harris smiled. “I might. I am thinking about it,” she said.

In recent months, apparently as an early step, Harris reportedly reached out to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and others on the Democratic left. She also called someone named James Zogby.

Zogby had been a leading voice warning Democrats in 2024 that their support for funding Israel’s war in Gaza would cost them the election. When Axios reported that Harris had privately called Zogby and others to try to mend the rift, he wouldn’t comment at the time. But in a recent interview, he confirmed the call to me—and said he liked what he heard. “We had a long talk,” he said, describing the call as Harris wanting to “correct the historical record” about what happened in 2024 and where her support lies. “I felt very—I felt very good about it. I think she’s a good person.”

I met Zogby—the head of the Arab American Institute and, at 80, a seasoned Arab activist—two years ago at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago. He was trying to convince a band of activists and around 30 delegates of the Uncommitted National Movement, representing some 700,000 voters opposed to the war, that the Democratic Party might actually be listening to them.

For the first time in the party’s history, he noted then, the DNC had officially sanctioned a panel on Palestinian human rights. Dr. Tanya Haj-Hassan, a pediatric intensive care physician who had volunteered in Gaza, described the horrific scenes she witnessed. Hala Hijazi, a longtime Democratic organizer, talked about relatives she had lost. Layla Elabed, one of the co-founders of the “uncommitted movement,” sat on the panel alongside Zogby, who had been having versions of this fight inside the Democratic Party for almost four decades. “We’ve come a long way,” he told the crowd, explaining what it meant that the conversation was happening at all. “It is something I do not want to dismiss for a minute as to how significant this is, about what message the Harris campaign is sending by saying, ‘We want to talk about this and hear you talk about it.’ ”

At the time, that did not sound entirely naive.

Joe Biden had dropped out of the race less than a month earlier. Harris had taken over the campaign, and people in the uncommitted movement were cautiously hopeful that that might mean a change in policy. Harris and her campaign had recently spoken privately with uncommitted organizers Elabed and Abbas Alawieh in Michigan. And behind the scenes, conversations continued over a particularly modest request: Let a Palestinian American be one of the 236 speakers to address the convention from the main stage.

They had spent months being told some version of the same thing: Donald Trump would be catastrophically worse for Palestinians, and therefore anything that endangered Harris was irresponsible. But they pressed ahead. “The people are with us on this,” Alawieh told me at the convention.

Change became harder to see as the week went on. The conversations behind the scenes at the convention culminated in Harris’ final answer for their request: no. There would be no Palestinian speaker. Protests broke out.

In her address to the convention, Harris did describe the suffering in Gaza as “devastating” and said Palestinians deserved “dignity, security, freedom, and self-determination.” That part received intense applause. It wasn’t enough. Harris lost Michigan to Trump by under 100,000 votes and lost the election. Trump returned to the White House. The activists I spoke to argued that Harris lost because she didn’t heed their warnings, though there was ultimately a lot that went wrong.

Since 2024, Democratic voters have moved substantially further away from Israel. Candidates attacking unconditional support for the Israeli government have won Democratic primaries. More than 100 House Democrats recently voted to eliminate billions in military assistance to Israel. And several of the people who spent the 2024 convention trying to convince Democrats that they were attempting to save the party, not sabotage it, have spent the intervening years burrowing further into Democratic politics.

Zogby told me he is still angry about what happened in 2024 but doesn’t squarely blame it on Harris’ position on Gaza. He mostly thinks the campaign failed by overrelying on political consultants and pollsters. He said he had reason to believe that Harris’ own instincts might have led somewhere different in that election but that she never had enough control over her own campaign to follow them. He had spoken with her earlier in the war, before she became the nominee, and told her to give a speech acknowledging what Palestinians were enduring and offering some recognition of their rights and their future. She told him she was already scheduled to speak that night. “Perfect. Do it. Work it in,” Zogby recalled telling her. When she told him the teleprompters were already prepared, he advised her to go off script. “Bill Clinton’s best lines were off script,” he said, laughing, as he recalled the conversation. The next day, he said, someone from her staff sent him a clip of Harris speaking about Palestinian rights.

Gaza, Zogby predicts, will play an outsized role in the upcoming election. “It’ll be a litmus test for ‘Are you ready for primetime or not?’ ” he said. “And not just ready for primetime in terms of the Middle East, but are you willing to stand up for a principled approach to foreign policy? Are you going to continue to mouth the nonsense that has gotten us into this hole and has discredited the Democratic Party in the eyes of its base for not being able to take a principled position not just on Gaza, but on so many other issues?

“We’re wimps,” Zogby said. “And one of the ways you show you’re not a wimp is Gaza, because that was the key way you became a wimp.”

Leaders of the 2024 uncommitted movement are also watching these developments carefully.

Elabed was among the Democratic activists organizing locally, then nationally. She and Alawieh briefly met Harris at a campaign stop near Detroit before the convention. Two years later, Elabed still remembers the encounter more favorably than someone hearing her criticisms of Harris might expect. “I always tell people, even to this day, when I spoke with her and I spoke about what my community was experiencing, what I personally was experiencing as a Palestinian American that had family in Palestine, her sympathy and empathy toward me and my community did feel really genuine,” she told me. “And I think that she was at that moment interested in talking more about the impact of U.S. funding to Israel on everyday people living here in Michigan and across the country, and what that meant for our families back home.”

Harris later wrote in her memoir 107 Days that she told Biden that his public comments about innocent Gazans could come across as “inadequate and forced.” She also wrote that activists threatening to withhold their votes had felt “reckless” to her.

I asked Elabed if she felt that line was directed at her. “I wish that her memoir was a little bit more telling,” she said. “I always wondered throughout her campaign why she would not deviate from Biden. Not just on the genocide, but, like, on any policy.”

Elabed told me that if Harris runs again, “I would hope that she would be able to run genuinely and authentically as herself, by herself.”

Headed into 2028, Congress is beginning to reflect the movement among Democratic voters. In July, Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who opposes foreign aid, prompted a House vote on eliminating $3.3 billion in annual assistance to Israel. The amendment failed 314–104. But 103 of the 104 votes to cut the aid came from Democrats—nearly half the caucus. That would have been unthinkable a decade ago.

The activist infrastructure has changed too. Alawieh, one of the people who spent the 2024 convention pressing Democrats for a Palestinian speaker, recently won the Democratic nomination for a Michigan state Senate seat. (Alawieh also got a call from Harris.) Abdul El-Sayed and other candidates running on staunch anti-war and economic-populist politics have won high-profile Democratic contests. The people who were standing outside the convention two years ago aren’t waiting outside anymore.

In a further sign of the times, this week, Harris endorsed El-Sayed and was stumping for him in Michigan.

Near the end of our conversation, I asked Zogby the question that hangs over Harris now. Given everything that happened, after what he heard on the call, did she really overcome 2024 and become the kind of candidate Democrats like him can support?

“I think she could,” Zogby said. “I do. I do, I do. I think she deserves the chance to do it. And I hope she takes advantage of that chance and does it.”

news.title: Voters trusted Republicans on immigration. Trump squandered it.
news.text:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Florida, has made waves by publicly breaking with President Donald Trump over immigration.

"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in a new campaign ad. "The same Hispanics that helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

In 2024, voters broadly trusted Republicans to handle illegal immigration. Through incompetence and cruelty, the Trump administration has lost that goodwill. The last election showed Republicans have a path forward on immigration. But to take it, they need to ditch the cruel memes and aggressive tactics that have plagued Trump's second term.

Salazar is right: Hispanics were a major part of Trump's 2024 victory. According to Pew Research Center, the president nearly tied former Vice President Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters, a group former President Joe Biden won by 25 percentage points in 2020. 

Since then, Trump's gains among Hispanics have evaporated. In February 2025, according to Pew, 93% of Hispanics who voted for Trump approved of the job he was doing. By April of this year, just 66% did. Over the same stretch, his approval among all Hispanic adults fell from 36% to 22%, while among non-Hispanic adults, it slipped from 49% to 37%.

The drop in support can be attributed largely to the administration's mishandling of immigration.

President Trump has fumbled immigration

The loudest headlines came out of Operation Metro Surge, the enforcement campaign that flooded Minneapolis with more than 3,000 federal agents last winter. The surge was driven more by political optics than by any strategic need, and it ended with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Worse yet, administration officials then smeared Pretti. White House advisor Stephen Miller called him a "domestic terrorist," and the Department of Homeland Security claimed he "wanted to do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement." Bystander video showed he never drew his holstered pistol, which he was licensed to carry. Americans noticed: 61% of voters told Quinnipiac University pollsters that the administration had not given an honest account of the shooting.

By mid-February, Americans opposed ICE's tactics 62% to 31%, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll. The backlash presumably helped cost Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem her job.

Since Noem's firing, ICE has largely faded from the headlines, as DHS Sec. Markwayne Mullin has worked to keep the agency out of the spotlight. That changed Sept. 20, when an ICE officer in Austin shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a Venezuelan man with a deportation order who had fled a vehicle stop. The facts are still unclear, and there is no ICE body-camera footage of the shooting. After Minneapolis, Americans have little reason to give the administration the benefit of the doubt.

Beyond the heated environment it needlessly created in Minnesota, the administration has driven support away with its messaging.

Throughout Trump's second term, official government social media accounts have churned out memes, many of them about immigration. The White House posted a Studio Ghibli-style cartoon of a convicted drug trafficker weeping as she was arrested and has promised that "the memes will continue." Other posts have included mock travel ads for deportation flights, and the administration has co-opted endless TikTok memes and audio trends to celebrate deportations.

All of it undercuts the administration's posture on such a serious matter. Nobody has ever been won over to a policy by a cartoon of a crying deportee, criminal or not. All it does is deepen the divide.

Republicans have a way forward on immigration, Hispanic voters

Frustration with Democrats' failures at the border handed Republicans an opening in 2024. Voters trusted Trump over Harris on immigration 51% to 38%. Republicans have since squandered that advantage, but the path to a sensible immigration policy isn't closed.

Americans still draw a line between securing the border and Trump's broader crackdown. In a New York Times/Siena College poll in January, roughly half of voters approved of his handling of the border, while they were split on deportations and a clear majority said ICE had "gone too far." That gap shows sensible border policy still has broad support, despite the administration's spectacle of mismanagement and cruelty.

Trump's inroads with Hispanic voters in 2024 were thought to signal a new Republican coalition, and they showed that these voters could back a more conservative immigration policy. Those gains have all but vanished. What looked like a lasting Republican asset has become a serious liability heading into the midterms.

To win back their advantage on immigration, Republicans need to ditch the cruelty. The memes, ICE's aggressive tactics and the general callousness have soured Americans on policies that should command popular support for years to come.

Lawmakers like Salazar may be breaking with Trump for electoral reasons. But if they win in November, they will be the ones building the Republican Party's next approach to immigration. That approach should press Democrats on their weaknesses on the issue, without the cruelty that has defined Trump's second term.

Dace Potas, a law student, is an opinion columnist for USA TODAY. Follow him on X: @DacePotas.

news.title: Trump presidency ‘as we know it’ ends in November – California governor
news.text:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has predicted that Democrats will regain control of the US House of Representatives in November, arguing that such an outcome would bring an end to Donald Trump’s presidency “as we know it.”

“We’re going to take back the House of Representatives. It’s a day of reckoning, a new day coming,” Newsom told AFP and two other media outlets after a UN climate summit in New York.

“Trump’s presidency, as we know it, ends in November,” said the 58-year-old outgoing Democratic governor of California, the most populous US state and one of the leading potential contenders for the Democratic Party’s 2028 presidential nomination.

Newsom made the remarks on Wednesday during an interview conducted as part of the Covering Climate Now journalism initiative. However, he did not explain specifically how a Democratic victory would effectively bring Trump’s presidency to an end.

If Trump’s Republicans lose control of one or both chambers of Congress, Democrats could restrict parts of the president’s legislative agenda, although the executive branch would still retain significant powers.

Newsom also argued that climate change could become a winning political issue if it is presented not simply as a “green” concern but as an issue connected to grocery prices, home insurance and national security.

“People say ‘why the hell are you talking about that, you should be talking about the kitchen table,’ I said ‘I am!’”

He cited the prices of beef and coffee, as well as difficulties surrounding home insurance and mortgages amid increasing climate risks, including more severe wildfires and coastal erosion intensified by El Nino.

California a green pioneer

According to Newsom, some politicians avoid discussing climate change because they struggle to communicate its relevance to voters.

He said politicians who have addressed the issue in the past have sometimes been portrayed as “soft, weak, effete, green, hyperbolic.”

Newsom acknowledged that “some of our language did get a little apocalyptic,” but argued that the focus should be on the wider economic and strategic implications.

The key, he said, is showing that “it’s not about electric power; it’s about economic power. It’s about statecraft.”

At the climate summit, Newsom presented California as an example of how climate action can coexist with economic growth. He said the state, which he described as the world’s fourth-largest economy, has seen its GDP grow by 40 percent since 2019 and had operated on 100 percent clean energy for at least part of the day on 90 percent of days this year.

His administration has also clashed with Trump and congressional Republicans over attempts to roll back California’s environmental regulations, including efforts to scrap the state’s planned phase-out of gasoline-powered cars and provide incentives for companies to abandon offshore wind projects.

“Donald Trump wants to recreate the 19th century,” Newsom said. “He’s doubling down on stupid. He’s putting America in reverse.”

“Whoever the nominee is of the Democratic Party is going to be the next president of the United States,” he added.

Newsom also said any Democratic presidential hopeful would be “exponentially better than a Rubio or Vance that have countenanced this corruption, this grift, this graft, this destruction of truth and trust and institutions,” referring to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance.

Rubio and Vance are widely viewed as potential Republican front-runners for 2028, although neither has formally declared a candidacy.

‘Old rules don’t apply’

Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez generated fresh speculation this week after telling The New York Times that she was considering a presidential bid.

She also questioned whether a Latina could win the presidency after female nominees were defeated in 2016 and 2024.

Ocasio-Cortez, Newsom and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff are among the names being discussed on betting markets.

Newsom said Ocasio-Cortez could potentially secure the Democratic nomination.

“She absolutely could become the nominee of the party. That’s my assessment of electability. This notion that a woman can’t win is insulting,” he said, blaming “punditry” for keeping the idea alive.

“I’m done with people talking like that. Or that if you’re from California or you’re Jewish or you’re old or you’re too young — give me a damn break. Our politics is completely scrambled post-Trump. The old rules, they do not apply.”

Although Newsom described Ocasio-Cortez as a “generational talent,” he did not rule out potentially competing against her.

Last week, he told CNN emphatically that he would not challenge Kamala Harris, the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024, with whom he has a long-standing relationship dating back to before either entered politics.

“It’s a different framework,” Newsom said. “I don’t have a relationship that goes back to before we were both in politics. I don’t have a relationship in the context of our base overlaying in remarkable ways.”

On whether he would ultimately seek the presidency, Newsom said his decision would depend on whether he could “look them and you in the eye and say I have something unique they don’t… voice, experience, perspective, capacity that is unique and distinctive.”

news.title: White House reinstates access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico following judge's order
news.text:
The White House said on Thursday it has reinstated journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico after a federal judge deemed US President Donald Trump’s ban of the three news outlets ​likely unconstitutional and ordered their access immediately restored.

The midday reinstatement came after a chaotic few hours earlier on Thursday when the journalists continued to be blocked from entering the White House grounds. That prompted ‌the three news organisations to request an immediate hearing before US District Judge Tim Kelly, who issued his decision overnight.

Kelly, acting in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Monday, ordered a halt to Trump’s ban for 14 days in a press freedom case that has played out over the past week in the courtroom and White House grounds.

Kelly found that the revocation of the White House credentials of the journalists “likely violated their constitutional due process rights.”

The judge, who Trump appointed in 2017 during his first presidential term, also raised doubts about the US Justice ​Department’s national security arguments for justifying the ban, noting that Trump himself had said the action was due to what the president alleged was false or negative coverage.

Hours after Kelly issued his order, CNN, MS NOW and ​Politico told the judge they remained barred, and asked for the emergency hearing. Politico said its reporter’s credentials were confiscated. An MS NOW reporter said she was blocked from the White House. CNN ⁠said some of its staff members were denied entry onto the grounds.

In response, Micah Stopperich, the director of press operations at the White House, said in a court filing that the White House began the process of reinstating press badges for ​affected reporters at 7:25 a.m., and that the “White House press team dropped badges at the entry gate for members of the press to pick up around 9:55 a.m.”

After receiving Stopperich’s declaration, the judge denied the request by the news organisations for an ​emergency hearing but gave them an opportunity to inform him of any factual developments later in the day.

The sharpest conflict yet between Trump and the press played out during a key diplomatic moment for the US president: his appearance at the United Nations General Assembly in New York and his hosting of Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

A source familiar with the White House television press pool said its members would not reinstate their coverage until the White House formally reinstates CNN to the pool. Earlier this week, they had suspended pooled coverage in solidarity with ​CNN.

There were no TV pool cameras set up for Xi’s arrival on the White House’s South Lawn on Thursday morning, and FOX News, MS NOW and CNN did not air the two leaders’ arrival ceremony live.

During Trump’s welcome of Xi to ​the White House, the president made a joke to photographers in the Oval Office about the Chinese having the friendliest press corps.

CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, FOX News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool. ‌They share the ⁠costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and provide footage to other outlets.

CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump’s trip to New York for the General Assembly on Monday but was not able to provide a pool feed.

NATIONAL SECURITY CONCERNS

Trump announced the ban on Friday on his social media platform, saying those news organisations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” Trump framed their reporting as a threat to US national security.

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration, saying the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. A coalition of press freedom groups and ​dozens of news organisations, including Reuters, later filed a legal brief ​supporting the three news outlets.

Kelly ordered the Trump administration ⁠to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and stop enforcing the ban for two weeks. The judge rejected the administration’s stated national security concerns.

“The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” Kelly ​wrote.

In a filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security with their coverage, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump’s White House ​ballroom and turnout at the recent ⁠Republican midterm convention.

Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the three outlets, welcomed the judge’s decision in a statement, saying: “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law.
We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”

TENSIONS WITH THE PRESS

Although other presidential administrations have battled with the press, Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented. Upending decades of tradition, his White House had denied basic access to many major news organisations, launched personal attacks on journalists and filed multiple lawsuits against news organisations.

Kelly’s ruling ⁠came a day ​after Trump experienced another legal setback.

On Wednesday, an Iowa judge dismissed Trump’s 2024 lawsuit against the Des Moines Register newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer. Trump ​sued the Register, its parent company Gannett and Selzer over a poll published ahead of the November 2024 US election that showed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris leading him in Iowa. Trump accused the newspaper and its longtime pollster of fraudulently misleading readers.

In his ruling Wednesday, Iowa District Judge Scott Beattie said ​the poll was legally protected speech.

news.title: Toward a Post-Trump Politics
news.text:
From the clutter of midterm election poll results, it's possible sometimes to see new patterns of political support emerging.

The overall pattern, as it stands, makes some sense. As in the 2006 and 2018 off-year cycles, the Republican president's job approval had sagged to well below 50 percent. Polls at this point in the year showed Democrats competitive in states and districts that the president had carried by solid margins two years before.

Democrats ended up gaining 30 House seats in 2006 and 41 in 2018, ousting Republican speakers and, in both elections, installing Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-CA). A similar result is expected this time, with Democrats needing to gain only three seats to win control, though Pelosi is retiring from Congress at age 86.

Such gains are not necessarily inevitable. Census redistricting ended up favoring Republicans. As Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini has pointed out, the summer polling understated Republicans' fall polling and November percentages in Senate races in 2014, 2018 and 2022. But he spots no similar move in polls conducted up through mid-September.

What I find striking is a sharp divergence in Senate polling between what have turned out to be seriously contested races in the North and in the South.

According to RealClearPolitics, in the South, Democrats have big leads in North Carolina (+8) and Georgia (+7). They narrowly lead in Texas (+2) and are only slightly behind in South Carolina (-3). In each state, they're polling far ahead of Trump 2024 benchmarks in North Carolina (Trump +3), Georgia (Trump +2), Texas (Trump +14) and South Carolina (Trump +18).

Overall, these Trump +9 Southern states are averaging +3 Democratic in Senate races — a big +12 Democratic swing.

The picture is different in four states up on the Canadian border. Democrats have only narrow edges in RealClearPolitics averages in Maine (+2), New Hampshire (+5), Michigan (+3) and Minnesota (+4). These numbers are in line with 2024 benchmarks in Maine (Harris +7), New Hampshire (Harris +3), Michigan (Trump +1) and Minnesota (Harris +4).

Overall, these four states that averaged Harris +3 are now averaging Democrats +3. No swing at all.

What accounts for the difference? One answer that quickly occurs is candidate selection.

Trump effectively chose the Republican nominees in the Southern races. He prompted the retirement of the occasionally anti-Trump incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and replaced him with the unknown Michael Whatley to run against a reputedly centrist two-term Democratic governor.

He issued a late endorsement of scandal-prone state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Texas Republican runoff rather than incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and evidently never considered the young Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-Texas), who ran third in the primary.

After the sudden death of incumbent South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham in July, Trump encouraged his inexperienced sister Darline Graham Nordone to run for the remainder of his term and endorsed her to run in November for a full term.

And while contesting the 2020 result in Georgia, Trump discouraged Republican turnout in the two January 2021 runoffs, which enabled Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Rafael Warnock (D-GA) to win 51 percent to 49 percent. Warnock won a full term against Trump-endorsed Herschel Walker by the same margin in 2022, and Ossoff seems headed for a bigger win this year. That gives the two Democrats 20 years in the Senate from a state that didn't elect a Democrat senator between 2000 and 2021.

Meanwhile, up by the Canadian border, left-wing and anti-Israel Democrat activists and primary voters have given their party's Senate nominations to candidates who, so far at least, are running behind former Vice President Kamala Harris's percentages in their states.

Running closest to Harris is Democratic Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who led primary polls by wide margins but won the primary by only 48.4 percent to 47.6 percent. A charismatic campaigner, he may have been hurt by bringing into his campaign the streamer Hasan Piker, who famously declared that America "deserved 9/11," and by responding to an attack on a synagogue in March by saying, "Hurt people hurt people."

Running further behind Harris is Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, winner of the Democratic-Farmer-Labor party nomination, who, as lieutenant governor, has been attacked for failure to prevent the hundreds of millions of dollars of Medicaid fraud by Somali immigrants.

The national spotlight has not been kind to Gov. Tim Walz (D-Minn.) since he was selected by Harris for the vice presidential nomination — his weak debate performance and the fraud perpetrated against his administration tarnished his party in a state whose many Scandinavian- and German-descended voters have been proud of the state's and the DFL's reputation for probity and competence.

Local and personal factors help explain Democrats' apparent difficulty in nailing down Senate wins in northern New England. In New Hampshire, John Sununu, son and brother of governors, won the same Senate seat in 2002 and lost it in 2008. The centrist record of his brother Chris Sununu, governor from 2017 to 2025, has made him surprisingly competitive in a high-education, Trump-averse state, which national Democrats have deprived of its first-in-the-nation presidential primary.

In Maine, Republican Susan Collins, after 30 years in the Senate, chairs the Appropriations Committee and has a moderate record, which helped her win reelection in 2020 by 51 percent to 42 percent after Democrat Sara Gideon outspent her two-to-one and led in every public poll.

This year, Democrats nominated Graham Platner, a Marine veteran and oysterman, though he turned out to have a Nazi tattoo and his only oyster customer was his mother's restaurant. Forced out by allegations of sexual harassment, he was replaced in September by logger Troy Jackson, whose working-class credentials seemed stronger but who had finished only third, with 21 percent, in the June primary for governor.

All of which looks like the beginning — the birthing pains, you might say — of a post-Donald Trump politics. The Republican polling firm Echelon Insights has been asking respondents whether they are "Trump-first" or "party-first" Republicans. In February 2025, a month after Trump's second inauguration and two months before his "liberation day" tariffs, Trump-first Republicans outnumbered party-firsters by a record 63 percent to 33 percent.

That was bound to decline at some point, and it has. This September, party-first Republicans, at 56 percent, significantly outnumbered Trump-first Republicans at 34 percent.

That inevitable process may have been sped up by Trump's stubborn preoccupation with issues of personal importance to him — putting his name on the Kennedy Center or demolishing it, the ballroom and triumphal arch, cryptocurrency — but of no value to the party or its voters, current and potential.

If I were a Democrat candidate, I'd consider plagiarizing the effective 2024 pro-Trump ad "Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you" with "Donald Trump is for him/his, this Democrat is for you."

In the meantime, Republicans, at least in the four northern Senate races mentioned here, seem to be getting in the habit of nominating candidates suited to local terrain and emphasizing issues tailored to their states — NFL commentator Michele Tafoya in Minnesota, seven-term congressman from a marginal district Mike Rogers in Michigan, and John Sununu in New Hampshire.

Gambling on many such candidates, as Democrat Rahm Emanuel did while heading his party's House campaign committee in the 2006 cycle, can be an effective way of expanding one's party to new constituencies.

In contrast, the Democrat Party today is saddled with a dominant faction, white college graduates, that demands obeisance to defense of wildly unpopular stands on cultural issues, from defunding the police to open-borders immigration to boys in girls' sports. Some even insist on sympathizing with the motives of those who launch armed attacks on synagogues.

Americans in the 21st century have, in increasing numbers, voted straight party tickets for or against candidates backing policies associated with George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Trump. How that works out depends on decisions not yet made and events that have not yet occurred.

Poll numbers have Democrats favored to win majorities in the House of Representatives and, by narrower margins, the Senate. But disparate regional trends suggest the Republicans may be getting a head start at what my Washington Examiner colleague Byron York calls "moving into the pro-Trump future."

Michael Barone is a senior political analyst for the Washington Examiner, resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and longtime co-author of The Almanac of American Politics. His new book, "Mental Maps of the Founders: How Geographic Imagination Guided America's Revolutionary Leaders," is now available.

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets' press passes and stop enforcing the ban for two weeks. The judge rejected the administration's stated national security concerns. "The record lacks factual support for defendants' contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security or ​that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds," Kelly wrote. In a filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security with their coverage, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump's White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican midterm convention. Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the three outlets, welcomed the judge's decision in a statement, saying: "This is ‌a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court's swift action." TENSIONS WITH THE PRESS Although other presidential administrations have battled with the press, Trump's campaign against the media has been unprecedented. Upending decades ‌of tradition, his White House had denied basic access to many major news organizations, launched personal attacks on journalists and filed multiple lawsuits against news organizations. Kelly's ruling came a day after Trump experienced another legal setback. On Wednesday, an Iowa judge dismissed Trump's 2024 lawsuit against the Des Moines Register newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer. Trump sued the Register, its parent company Gannett and Selzer over a poll published ahead of the November 2024 US election that showed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris leading him in Iowa. Trump accused the newspaper and its longtime pollster of fraudulently misleading readers. In his ruling Wednesday, Iowa District Judge Scott Beattie said the poll was legally protected speech.
news.summary: The White House restored access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico after a federal judge ruled that Trump's ban likely violated their constitutional rights

news.title: Trump’s US ratings drop to new record low as Democrats become clear favourites in both chambers of Congress
news.text:
In Nate Silver’s aggregate of national polls, Donald Trump’s net approval has dropped to a new record low of -23. 

In his forecast model, Democrats are the clear favourites to gain control of the US federal Senate at November 3 midterm elections, and overwhelming favourites to gain control of the House of Representatives.

If disruption caused by the Iran war continues until the midterm elections, with increased petrol prices and inflation, Republicans are likely to lose control of both the House and the Senate, perhaps with huge losses.

However, if the disruption eases again and petrol prices fall back before the midterms, I believe Republicans will do better than they are now and may retain control of the Senate.

I can say this because Trump’s net approval and the generic ballot were better for Republicans in early September, soon after a low in petrol prices.

Trump’s ratings

In analyst Nate Silver’s aggregate of US national polls, Trump’s net approval is at a new record low -23.0. Currently, 60.4% disapprove of his performance and 37.4% approve.

Trump’s net approval was -19.7 in my September 14 article. It had improved to -18.7 on September 4 before falling back.

Trump’s net approval is below what any past president since Harry Truman had at this point in their term, with Trump’s first term the closest at -11.6.

On four issues tracked by Silver, Trump’s net approval is -13.0 on immigration, -28.3 on trade, -32.1 on the economy and -46.4 on inflation. Since my September 14 article, Trump’s net approval on immigration, trade and the economy have all dropped one to two points.

Silver also has an aggregate of US support for the Iran war. Currently, 57.9% are opposed to the Iran war while 33.5% support it, for a net support of -24.4, down from -20.1 in my September 14 article.

Midterm elections on November 3

All 435 federal House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 senators will be up for election at November 3 midterm elections.

In 2024 elections, Republicans won the House by 220–215 over Democrats and the Senate by 53–47. Owing to Vice President JD Vance’s potential tie-breaking vote, Democrats need at least a four-seat gain to win Senate control.

I previously wrote that, owing to Republican gerrymandering, Democrats need at least a four-point margin in the generic ballot to have a good chance to win the House majority. The Senate is more skewed to Republicans as every state has two senators. Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win the Senate on a uniform swing.

In Silver’s midterm election forecast model, the generic ballot gives Democrats a 51.4–42.3 lead over Republicans, a 9.1-point margin (8.2 points in my September 14 article). Democrats’ lead had dropped to 7.4 points on September 4.

Polls that screen for likely voters usually give Democrats larger leads than polls that ask registered voters. Democrats are more likely to vote at lower turnout elections like the midterms than Republicans, when Trump is not on the ballot.

Silver’s model gives Democrats a 69% chance to win the Senate and a 91% chance to win the House, respectively 57% and 86% on September 14. Democratic chances to win the Senate had fallen to a low of 50% on September 7, and their chances of winning the House had dropped to 81% on September 3.

While uniform swing indicates that Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win control of the Senate, Silver’s model has Democrats as the favourites to win with a 6–7 point margin in the generic ballot. In the House, Democrats are favourites if they win by 3–4 points.

Democrats now lead by two to five points in Senate contests in Texas, Ohio, Alaska and Iowa. Trump won all these states by double-digit margins in 2024. This explains why Democrats are the favourites to gain control of the Senate. Furthermore, Republicans are trailing an independent in Nebraska by 0.2 points and only leading a Democrat in Kansas by 1.3 points.

A bad spot for Democrats is Maine, which should be the easiest Senate gain for them as Kamala Harris defeated Trump in Maine by 6.9 points. But Republican incumbent Susan Collins has led Democrat Troy Jackson in the last two Maine Senate polls, including a three-point lead in a Siena poll for The New York Times.

The two key items that could go wrong for Democrats are a markedly improved economy by November for most Americans – not just the stock market – and a systematic error in which Republicans overperform the polls.

Economic data

Americans are currently paying an average of US$4.48 (A$6.69) a gallon for regular petrol (gasoline in the US). Owing to profits and taxes, the retail price of petrol will be higher than the commodity price. 

The commodity price of petrol has surged from a low of US$2.99 (A$4.27) a gallon on August 27 to US$3.49 (A$4.89) now, but down from US$3.52 (A$5.02) on Wednesday. The Iran war high was US$3.76 (A$5.36) on May 18. Before the Iran war began, it was under US$2.

In Silver’s models, Trump and Republicans were at a high in early September, shortly after the August 27 low point in petrol prices.

There appears to be a lag time from changes in the oil price being passed on to petrol. The international benchmark Brent oil peaked at US$108.75 (A$155.17) a barrel on September 15, but fell to US$99.25 (A$141.61) on Tuesday before rising to its current US$105.81 (A$150.97). This implies there should be at least a short-lived drop in petrol prices soon.

After large gains in the three sessions from September 17–21, the benchmark US S&P stock market index is down just 1.2% from its August 13 peak, but up 10.9% from its peak in the week before the Iran war began in late February. It’s up 16.9% from its worst point in the Iran war in late March.

While the AI boom is assisting the stock market, Silver said a poll for Politico had 63% thinking there was at least a moderate risk of AI destroying humanity, compared with 22% who thought there was no or a very small risk. The splits between Trump and Harris 2024 voters were not wide, with Trump voters favouring at least a moderate risk by 61–29 and Harris voters by 70–21.
news.summary: Trump’s net approval is below what any past president since Harry Truman had at this point in their term.

news.title: 'Where do we go from here?' Trump's flouting of court order flabbergasts analysts
news.text:
Analysts were left aghast and thinking about how to reckon with President Donald Trump's insistence on banning certain media outlets from the White House.

During a Thursday segment on CNN, Jamal Simmons, the former communications director for VP Kamala Harris, said that Trump's defiance of the law will force the American people to consider what matters. The discussion came after CNN White House correspondent Kristen Holmes was restricted from the White House despite a judge's temporary order blocking Trump's media ban.

"The American people deserve a free press. They deserve a freedom of speech. We fought a revolution for that. We fought a civil war so that we could give those rights to other people. We had World War II to defend democracy," Simmons explained. "At this point, it's time for all of us to have a really, really frank conversation about where do we go from here and what kind of principles tie us together around these freedoms?"

Former Trump White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham said that she knew Trump would ignore the order and block a correspondent from entering the White House because he would always push back as much as he can.

She predicted that the Trump White House's "next steps will be that they're going to try to put some kind of due process in place because the courts keep leaning on that, and it's going to be something that tries to box the media into, like I said, no correspondent or no shouting questions or something along those lines."

She was referring to how U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who issued the temporary restraining order blocking the media ban, wrote that the White House needs a procedure in place before it starts kicking journalists out.

Grisham slammed the White House for refusing to let reporters into the White House despite Kelly's ruling, saying, "What they did was dishonest."

news.title: Chris Pappas Reverses Polling Trend in New Hampshire Senate Race
news.text: In the New Hampshire race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democrat Chris Pappas has reversed a recent polling trend in his battle against Republican John E. Sununu, a new survey from the University of New Hampshire shows on Thursday. U.S. Representative Pappas now leads 50 percent to Sununu's 42 percent, after the Republican was found ahead with the pollster in August. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during midterm elections. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen is set to retire, opening the seat for November's general election. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won New Hampshire in the 2024 presidential election over President Donald Trump by under 3 percent. The state has notably not elected a Republican senator in over 15 years. Sununu represented the Granite State in the Senate from 2003 to 2009. Newsweek reached out to Pappas and Sununu's campaigns via email on Thursday for comment on the new poll. What To Know According to the new poll, 50 percent would pick Pappas, 42 percent would pick Sununu, 2 percent would pick Constitution Party candidate Edmond Laplante, 2 percent would write in another candidate and 4 percent are undecided. Pappas' favorability rating in the new poll is 33 percent compared to a 47 percent unfavorable rating, 17 percent are neutral and 3 percent do not know enough to say either way. Sununu's favorability rating is 34 percent versus a 49 percent unfavorable rating, while 13 percent are neutral and 4 percent don't know enough to say either way. The University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll was conducted from September 17 to September 21 among 1,418 likely general election voters, with a margin of error of 2.6 percent. In an August survey from the pollster, Sununu was up 45 percent compared to 43 percent for Pappas, 5 percent would have voted for another candidate and 7 percent were undecided. The poll was conducted from August 20 to August 24 among 1,878 likely general election voters, with a margin of error of 2.3 percent. The results for this survey were within the margin of error, making it a statistical tie. A co/efficient poll earlier this month also had the race deadlocked between the two at 46 percent, while 9 percent were undecided. Pappas' favorability was 37 percent compared to a 51 percent unfavorable rating and 13 percent had no opinion. Sununu's favorability was 41 percent compared to a 47 percent unfavorable rating and 12 percent had no opinion. The poll was conducted from September 9 to September 11 among 958 likely general election voters in the Granite State and had a margin of error of 3.15 percent. A survey from GOP pollster Fabrizio, Lee & Associates last month showed the contest in a statistical tie with Sununu obtaining 37 percent of the potential vote compared to Pappas' 36 percent. The poll showed that 23 percent were undecided while other candidates garnered less than 4 percent. The poll was conducted from August 27 to August 30 among 600 likely voters in the state and had a 4 percent margin of error. The new poll released on Thursday shows a flip in possible momentum for Democrats less than six weeks out from Election Day. Earlier this month, however, Cook moved the contest from Lean Democratic to a Toss-Up amid the competitive polling. The race has also caught the eye of Republicans nationally, who are on pace to hold a $20 million edge in the state, Cook notes. "Sununu allies have already outspent pro-Pappas groups by almost a 2-1 margin," the forecaster highlighted in part. Map Shows Senate Toss-Up Races Ahead of Midterms Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The new poll shows a flip in possible momentum in Democrats' favor less than 6 weeks out from Election Day.

news.title: Is rural Minnesota more conservative than rural Iowa and Wisconsin?
news.text:

Rural Minnesota counties were redder than Iowa and Wisconsin’s rural counties in the 2024 presidential election.

Definitions of rural vary depending on the source, but a federal classification of metro and nonmetro counties allows for clear comparisons. In Minnesota, metro counties are mostly those encompassing or near the Twin Cities, Rochester, Duluth, St. Cloud, Mankato and Moorhead.

Voters in nonmetro Minnesota counties, considered rural for these purposes, cast ballots for President Donald Trump by a nearly 30% margin over Kamala Harris in 2024. Comparable counties in Iowa had 29% margins in favor of Trump, while he won by 23% in Wisconsin’s rural counties.

The state with the reddest individual counties, however, was Iowa. The Hawkeye State had four counties with more than 60% margins for Trump. Minnesota’s largest margin for Trump was 56% in Morrison County.

news.title: 'Assassination' post draws condemnation from all sides
news.text:
The Libertarian Party of New Hampshire, which is unaffiliated with the national party, received widespread condemnation Thursday for a social media post supporting violence against Democratic leaders.

The post made Wednesday on X said, “We openly support the assassination of basically every elected Democrat in New Hampshire. But if you don’t have the balls to do that then you should probably vote GOP.”

It also had a follow-up post: “LPNH believes that New Hampshire is healthier and freer when anyone who would enact an income tax fears for their life.”

In March, LPNH posted on X that killing former N.H. Executive Councilor Andru Volinsky would be permissible because of his support for an income tax. In 2024, it had a post praising anyone who assassinated then-Vice President Kamala Harris.

Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte decried Wednesday’s post.

“This type of behavior is irresponsible and dangerous,” she said in a statement. “Violent rhetoric has no place in our politics, and threats like this should be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

A spokesman for the N.H. Attorney General’s office emailed a brief statement:

“We can confirm that the New Hampshire Department of Justice is aware of the social media posts. We would not be in a position to comment further at this time.”

LPNH Chairman Jeremy Kauffman posted Thursday a notification from X that the service had temporarily locked the LPNH account for breaking the rules of the social media site. The rules of X prohibit posts “explicitly threatening, inciting, glorifying, or expressing desire for violence.”

The national Libertarian Party said in its own post that it opposes political violence, had ended its affiliation with the New Hampshire organization in May and had designated the Granite State Libertarian Party as its affiliate in the state.

“All members of the Libertarian Party are required to take the Libertarian Party Membership Pledge: ‘I hereby certify that I oppose the initiation of force as a means of achieving political or social goals,’” the national organization said.

“Political and social change must be pursued through peaceful, voluntary means — not violence, threats, or aggression.”

Since its decertification in May, it’s not clear how many people still belong to the LPNH, which said it had 130 credentialed members at its annual convention in March.

Deputy Speaker of the N.H. House Steven Smith, R-Charlestown, and House Minority Leader Alexis Simpson condemned the LPNH post.

Smith called it “unhinged and unacceptable.

“No matter your party, political violence has zero place in New Hampshire, period. We need to drop this garbage, get back to regular debating, and settle our differences the right way.”

Simpson said “every leader has a responsibility to reject this dangerous rhetoric. No one should fear for their life because of their beliefs or their decision to serve the people of New Hampshire.”

N.H. Rep. Nicholas Germana of Keene, the Democratic deputy House floor leader, said that while the NHLP comments “do not represent most libertarians, and I know they do not represent most of the Republicans I work with in Concord, the fact is that this kind of rhetoric has been normalized within the GOP from the President of the United States to the NH House majority leader.”
news.summary: The Libertarian Party of New Hampshire, which is unaffiliated with the national party, received widespread condemnation Thursday for a social media post supporting violence against Democratic leaders.
news.author: Rick Green

news.title: The 2028 implications of Michigan’s Senate race: From the Politics Desk
news.text: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen explains why Democrats with presidential aspirations will be paying close attention to the outcome of the Michigan Senate election. Plus, Alexandra Marquez identifies an issue that has united candidates in both parties in tight races. — Adam Wollner The 2028 implications of Michigan’s Senate race Analysis by Jonathan Allen Potential Democratic presidential hopefuls are starting to make sure they find their way to Michigan to campaign for Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Former Vice President Kamala Harris was there this week. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a former South Bend, Indiana, mayor who now lives in Michigan, appeared with El-Sayed in August. And Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., has said he’ll be on the trail next month with El-Sayed, a darling of the left wing of the party. It’s less about him than it is about them. That’s because El-Sayed presents a bit of a twofer in the endorsement game: 2028 contenders can cozy up to the left and advance the party’s goal of retaking the Senate. Whether El-Sayed wins or loses, those who campaigned with him will surely take credit for both the former and the latter come presidential primary season. The other thing that is as certain as death and taxes is that El-Sayed’s performance against Republican Mike Rogers this fall will be treated within Democratic circles as a sign of whether to sprint left or hit the brakes in 2028. After all, Michigan is a crucial swing state, and, if El-Sayed wins, progressives will argue that they have proven a Bernie Sanders acolyte can capture the presidency. He might not even have to win for that case to be made. On the other hand, more mainstream Democrats would take a defeat — flipping a Democratic seat into Republican hands — as a proof point that voters in battleground states aren’t willing to swing too far left. There’s some recent history here. In 2018, the waiting-in-the-wings class of 2020 Democratic hopefuls read anti-Donald Trump enthusiasm and primary victories by upstart progressives as clarion calls to race to the left. Some of them signed up for Sanders’ “Medicare for All” legislation. In the end, though, Joe Biden — who resisted “Medicare for All” and pleas to defund the police — won both the Democratic nomination and the presidency. Did he prove a progressive couldn’t become president? Of course not. But Democratic voters were concerned, after four years of Trump, that they might blow the 2020 election by nominating a more liberal candidate. It’s not yet clear whether they will feel the same way in 2028. But potential Democratic presidential candidates and their aides will keep a close watch on El-Sayed’s performance — even when they’re not campaigning with him — as they try to gauge how to position themselves best for the primary and the general election. 🔴 On the other side of the aisle: Michigan Republicans break with Trump on Iran, AI and data centers, by Allan Smith and Sahil Kapur How corruption is popping up in Republican and Democratic ads everywhere By Alexandra Marquez Amid a knock-down, drag-out fight for control of Congress, one issue is dominating advertising and transcending partisan divides, instead pitting challengers against incumbents: Everyone is running against members of Congress trading stocks. At least one TV or digital ad mentioning the issue has run in the last month in nearly every competitive race for Congress, according to an analysis of AdImpact data. That includes 18 of the 21 House races rated as “toss-ups” by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter and all but one Senate race rated as a “toss-up” or “leaning” slightly toward one party. Members of both parties are campaigning against congressional stock trading, attacking incumbents and alleging they have used their perch in Congress to get rich amid a broader affordability crisis in the U.S. And unlike some other political issues, it’s just as useful in a battleground district as it is in a deeper red or blue district, as independents and voters from both parties throw up their hands at allegations of government corruption. In some places, members of Congress are airing ads promoting support for a ban on stock trading while an opponent or super PAC runs ads tallying up trades the incumbent made, according to public financial disclosures. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
news.summary: Jonathan Allen explains why Democrats with presidential aspirations will be paying close attention to the outcome of the Michigan Senate election.
