news.title: Jon Husted in Dead Heat Against Sherrod Brown as He Breaks With Trump
news.text: Republican Senator Jon Husted and former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, are locked in a dead heat in the latest poll of the Ohio U.S. Senate race released on Thursday. The race is expected to be one of the most competitive races of this year's midterms and could end up deciding whether Democrats or Republicans win control of the upper chamber of Congress. Although Ohio backed President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024, Democrats see the race as competitive due to a stronger national environment and the candidacy of Brown, who has won statewide in the past despite the state’s rightward drift. The new poll pointed to a tight race. Brown’s support stood at 45.6 percent, while Husted had the backing of 45.3 percent of respondents—a statistical tie. Other candidates received about 3.5 percent of the vote, while 5.5 percent were undecided, according to the poll, which surveyed 695 likely voters September 21-23 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. Brown had a large advantage among unaffiliated voters, winning by 17 points, 51 percent to 34 percent, the poll found. The poll comes just days after Husted broke with Trump to call for an end to the Iran war, which has become a vulnerability for Republicans ahead of the midterms. "The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices," Husted told Politico on Tuesday. Newsweek reached out to the Brown and Husted campaigns for comment via email. Jon Husted vs. Sherrod Brown: What Latest Polls Say The Ohio race is a special election after Husted was appointed to fill the seat previously held by Vice President JD Vance. Brown, who lost reelection in 2024, is running to make a comeback in Ohio, a former battleground that has become more conservative in the Trump era. The Quantus Insights poll is in line with other recent surveys showing a competitive race, though most polls have given Brown a modest lead. Brown was up by 3 points in a survey from Bowling Green State University and YouGov. He received support from 48 percent of respondents to 45 percent for Husted. It surveyed 1,000 likely voters September 1-10 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. An InsiderAdvantage poll gave Brown a 5-point advantage, 47 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters September 8-9, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. The Democratic candidate also led a Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, by 8 points, 53 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 1,008 registered voters August 6-10, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points. However, Husted led an earlier poll, released by The New York Times and Siena University, by 3 points, 50 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 601 likely voters June 15-28, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. Latest Developments in the Race The race has drawn notable investments from the crypto industry. The crypto-backed super PAC Fairshake is set to spend at least $30 million against Brown in November, according to a report from The New York Times. The investment comes after the Senate Democrats opposed a procedural vote on the Trump-backed CLARITY Act, which would create a federal regulatory framework for cryptocurrencies and other digital assets. Patrick Eisenhauer, Brown’s campaign manager, said Husted was "for sale and the billionaires and corporations pouring millions into this race know it." "Of course the special interests are panicking, they know Sherrod will fight the rigged system they’re feasting on to stand up for working Ohioans," Eisenhauer told Newsweek in an emailed statement. Olivia Tripodi, press secretary for Husted's Senate office, told Newsweek that he believes the bill would establish clear rules for cryptocurrency, protect consumers and support domestic innovation and job creation. "Senator Husted believes that, if the U.S., not China, is going to lead in global banking and digital assets, the U.S. needs a framework that is clear, practical and supports innovation and job creation here at home," Tripodi said, adding he was disappointed that Senate Democrats had blocked the measure. How Have the Campaigns Been Financed? Husted’s campaign announced in July that he raised $7.7 million in the second quarter of 2026, with more than $11 million cash on hand. Meanwhile, Brown’s campaign said he raised more than $17.1 million in the same period. Why the Ohio Senate Race Matters in the Midterms The race is one of a handful of toss-ups that could determine the balance of power in the Senate. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority that is seen as increasingly at risk in November. Democrats must flip four seats to win a majority, as Vance would serve as the tiebreaker in a 50-50 Senate. Democrats are defending seats they hold in Trump-won states like Georgia and Michigan, as well as a seat in light-blue New Hampshire. They view GOP-held seats in Maine and North Carolina as their top targets. But no other GOP-held seats are up for grabs in states that Trump won by single digits or outright lost, so Democrats have to turn to more conservative states to find those last two seats. Polls suggest their best opportunities are in states like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas. If Democrats win Ohio, their path to a Senate majority becomes narrower, but if Husted wins, that means they would need to win in some of those other states to win control of the chamber. Sherrod Brown Eyes Comeback Brown is hoping to reverse trends in Ohio that have favored Republicans over the past decade. For much of the 2000s, Ohio was a swing state willing to back members of both parties. It voted for President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, but went on to support Trump three times, including by 11 percentage points in 2024. Trump made inroads with white, working-class voters who were previously more divided. His gains came from rural counties as well as the northeastern region near Cleveland. Democrats have gained some ground in Cincinnati and Columbus suburbs, but not enough to offset Republican gains in the rural areas. But notably, Brown won reelection in 2018, Trump’s first midterm. He also overperformed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, losing by fewer than 4 points. Democrats hope that a better national environment, fueled by growing disapproval of Trump, can help pull him across the finish line. Ohio also has a competitive gubernatorial race this year, with polls showing a toss-up between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. What Happens Next The Ohio Senate race is going to be watched closely over the coming weeks. It’s not clear whether Brown and Husted will face off in a debate before the election. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classify the race as a pure toss-up. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Dave Siminoff.

news.title: Working The 'Polls': Content Creators Spot A Creative, Spicy Way To Recruit Election Workers
news.text:
Soapy car washes, bikini photo shoots and pole dancing are taking over this year’s midterm elections.

Political content creators are making suggestive winks and sharing thirst traps in a spicy campaign to help boost civic engagement as election jurisdictions continue to report difficulties recruiting poll workers.

“Did I see myself a month ago slowly emerging from a pool as water careened off my body? Did I see myself finding a stripper pole somewhere in West Hollywood?” progressive political commentator Brian Tyler Cohen told HuffPost with a chuckle. “No, but I think that you have to be creative in this moment.”

As President Donald Trump undermines confidence in U.S. elections in the lead-up to November, creators told HuffPost that they’re using sexiness to sell their followers on the critical role poll workers play in democracy. Cohen is leading the push through Chorus, a nonprofit he co-founded that works with “pro-democracy creators.”

Political influencers have been spotted taking off their shirts, posing with dancing poles and dropping “thirst traps for democracy” in hopes of getting their followers to sign up to staff their local polling places by greeting voters, issuing ballots and otherwise supporting the democratic process. They’re also encouraging followers to check their voter registrations.

While poll worker recruitment proved to be “easier” in 2024 compared with the 2020 election, 48% of election jurisdictions reported difficulties in recruiting and retaining a “sufficient” number of workers at locations, per a report from the bipartisan U.S. Election Assistance Commission.

Cohen said that, as of earlier this week, the thirst trap trend has led to 31,000 poll worker interest forms being completed at Power the Polls — a nonpartisan initiative that describes itself as recruiting the “next generation of poll workers.”

There have also been over 60,000 voter registration checks as a result of the creators’ posts, per Cohen.

Alexandra Cascio — who shared a snap of herself in lingerie with a glittery red backdrop to tease what “no one tells you” about being a paid poll worker earlier this month — said Chorus called on scores of creators in July to take part in the recruitment efforts.

Inspired by a “click-baity” post by Elizabeth Booker Houston directing her followers to ways to protest Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Cascio used a picture from an old boudoir photo shoot to urge people to stop Trump’s efforts to “steal the 2026 midterms.”

“It’s almost leaning into the ways we know the internet operates, right? The more clickbaity, the more ‘gotcha,’ you can actually get views and attention,” Cascio said, referring to a need to “gamify” the algorithm to excite people about a “dry” topic like poll worker recruitment.

In a video earlier this month, attorney A.B. Burns-Tucker thanked the 2,100 people who had completed poll worker interest forms after she posted a clip of herself in a bikini, adding, “I know I had to show a little ‘mmm’ to get y’all attention but the reality is that, when it came down to it, you stepped up.”

Other creators have found creative ways to take part in the push, as well.

Tevin Davis — known for his viral Kamala Harris impersonations — played with the word “poll” in several posts, including one that starts with a clip of a woman falling as she tries to dance on a pole.

“It truly just became a thing that allowed people to feel like there could be joy, there could be humor, but that they had tangible information that they can then take and then turn it into civic engagement,” he said of the campaign.

Sam Rosenholtz, better known as Good Trouble to his 1.4 million followers, has worked the pole, too and gotten into what he calls a “thirst trap-off” with Cohen in recent weeks.

“More poll workers means more polling places can be open, more infrastructure can be had. That is a real world, tangible sort of answer to some of the apathy, some of the worry about voting on the day, and that directly translates into positivity about voting,” Rosenholtz stressed.

news.title: 'A Communism of Pelf': How Trump betrayed American workers
news.text:
President Donald Trump's trade wars with Canada and Europe — who have traditionally been American allies — are more than merely "weird' (to quote economist Dr. Ed Gresser), although they are most certainly that. They have simultaneously done three things, all of them profoundly negative for both Americans and the rest of the world: First, they have raised prices for American workers while making their jobs less secure; second, they have hurt the United States' standing in the global community; and third, they have created a political culture rife with corruption.

Or, to quote President Grover Cleveland: Instead of creating a communism of the proletariat, they have instead established a "communism of pelf."

These ideas are not always easy to communicate to the general public, which is why AlterNet was grateful to speak with Dr. Elizabeth McKillen, professor emerita of history at the University of Maine. McKillen specializes in US history, labor history and foreign policy history, and has written two well-received monographs, "Making the World Safe for Workers: Labor, the Left, and Wilsonian Internationalism" and "Chicago Labor and the Quest for a Democratic Diplomacy: 1914-1924." In the subsequent conversation, McKillen illuminates how Trump's trade policies are fundamentally changing the world as we have known it for generations.

This interview has been lightly edited for accuracy, clarity, context and length.

How Trump hurts America's positive influence in the world.

ROZSA: You've written about President Woodrow Wilson, who, through the philosophy known as Wilsonianism, promoted liberal democratic internationalism to create a world order defined by national sovereignty, a rule of law, and the promotion of peace. How did Wilsonianism alter America's standing worldwide, and how has Trumpism changed that?

McKILLEN: Well, that's an interesting historical question. I noticed you had a background in history. I think there's a large gap of time there, but initially, of course, Wilsonian internationalism was not that influential, because the Senate rejected the treaty and, therefore, the League of Nations... There was, of course, that isolationist sentiment during the '30s, so we were slow to enter World War II. But in the aftermath of World War II, we did see a period of free trade and a period in which the U.S. assumed a kind of hegemonic mantle and worked with international organizations for a period of time.

And so I think that Trump has rejected that role on many levels. I shouldn't say he's rejected hegemony, or that role of the United States being influential in affairs; it's just that he wants to play more the bully, as opposed to engaging in international cooperation. So that's one thing that's different. And then he has, of course, rejected free trade and moved us back to protectionism, which flourished in the '30s and arguably made the Depression much worse. For that reason, there were many of us who were always skeptical about tariffs as a way to renew American prosperity, and of course that's proven to be true. It's alienated our allies throughout the world, including Canada, perhaps previously one of our closest trade partners.

So those are the things that come to me off the top of my head. I do think he's rejected elements of that. He's also rejected elements of closing the gap between rich and poor, both domestically and internationally, which there was some interest in during the post-World War II period, at least in the U.S. helping out struggling economies. That happened in Europe first, through the Marshall Plan, because we were concerned that Europe revive. And then it happened later in underdeveloped countries through USAID. Of course, that was not entirely altruistic on the part of the United States, because what it realized is that its own economic well-being, to some degree, now depended upon a global market for its goods. And so the United States increasingly came during the Cold War, ironically, to see that kind of outreach to struggling economies as necessary to maintaining its own economic growth.

But Trump has largely rejected that as a kind of charity and has argued that the United States needs to give less of its funds to international uplift, so to speak. And so that has been another element of contest between him and European allies. It's also applied even to issues of international health, of course, as things like Ebola have surfaced in Africa, and how much do you help African countries to overcome that? We slashed some of those funds, so that's problematic as well. So, in essence, yes, Trump said he was returning to an America First strategy, although you could argue that an America First strategy has not served America very well because of the rise of a global economy.

The other thing that happened by the '70s, of course, was that the rest of the world caught up with us, or part of the world caught up with us, and we had rivalry in economic terms between the United States and Japan and the United States and Europe. So then the question was how you deal with that. A lot of American companies tended to want to go find the lowest-wage markets around the world, whereas labor and other groups started to argue that, no, you needed to emphasize the home market and pay workers enough money so that they could afford American products. And so there was a kind of anti-Japanese revolt, if you will, among labor even in the '70s, because they objected to everybody buying Japanese cars and wanted the American automobile industry to remain very strong.

So those are a few things that come to me off the top of my head.

How Trump hurts American workers.

ROZSA: Can you explain how President Donald Trump's trade wars, particularly with Canada and the European Union, are hurting American workers? I am asking this question in two ways. First, how is it hurting American workers in terms of raising prices? And second, how is the trade war hurting American workers in terms of their labor rights?

McKILLEN: Well, in terms of what it costs American workers, it's pretty clear that those kinds of tariffs ultimately cause higher prices for workers when they go to buy something. That's, of course, because Trump really lied in his election campaign about how foreign countries paid for tariffs, and that's not true. It tends to be, first, the businesses in America that buy foreign goods, and then, secondly, they tend to pass that on to consumers. So that part of Donald Trump's argument was always untrue, and I had published some stuff in the local press about that. But the other element of it, I think, was more convincing to American workers initially, which is that you wanted to bring American industry back home if it had moved away.

There was that runaway-plant phenomenon in the '70s and '80s, and so people initially tended to buy that. That was true even, for example, of Shawn Fain of the United Auto Workers. Despite the fact that he had initially given a campaign speech for Kamala Harris, he then turned over and liked the tariff approach of Trump. But as we've seen, that also didn't work, because, of course, factory jobs have actually declined because of the tariffs. Part of that is because even American factories that are making goods rely on foreign products to make them. And then it tended to raise the prices of their goods, too. So those things hurt workers. And if you're talking about Canada, for example, there are really good examples of how the auto industries in the United States and Canada were very much intertwined, and so those hurt workers too.

Now, I argue that the other way in which Trump's policies have hurt American workers is that, clearly, he's engaged in some kinds of union busting in terms of federal workers, and that's a big proportion of the population. And then also, he's done terrible things with the National Labor Relations Board, as he did with a lot of independent agencies. He fired the person who was in charge of that board. Those federal agencies, all of them, I think, really need to remain independent, but he has compromised their independence. In the case of the National Labor Relations Board, it's been largely disempowered, because he has not replaced that person that he fired, and so it hasn't been able to do anything because it doesn't have a quorum. And the National Labor Relations Board has, since the 1930s, clearly been quite important in guaranteeing workers' rights to unions on the job.

So I would say that those are some of the ways in which Donald Trump has really hurt the rights of workers.

ROZSA: The Supreme Court has repeatedly ruled Trump's tariffs to be illegal, yet he keeps imposing them. How does this undermine America's economic standing in the global community?

McKILLEN: Well, I think it makes the global community, needless to say, feel insecure about its future relations with the United States. And economists of course, say that that's the worst thing that can happen; even steady high tariffs are better than not knowing what the future will bring. So I think that's problematic. And then I think also that many in the international community have recognized that tariffs are hurting all workers. They hurt workers in the United States, and they hurt workers in other countries.Now, there are periods in the history of each country where there's a need for a certain level of protectionism. The best case for that in the United States is probably the era immediately after the American Revolution, because American industry was behind British industry, and so we really needed a few protective tariffs. I'm not arguing there should never be protective tariffs, but they need to be focused, and they do need to be reciprocal, and they really have not been in Trump's case, whatever he argues. He instead tends to play this role of world bully, and I think everyone resents it.

And also, his economic knowledge just seems so poor that foreign countries often make fun of him. This is certainly true of Canada, for example, where they named a washroom after him, or even Ireland, where they have a statue of him sitting in a garbage can. So he displays this kind of astounding lack of knowledge of basic economic principles, or people either believe that or they believe that he's just lying. And so he's really viewed as kind of a farce, and I don't think people abroad terribly understand him, or understand why Americans would vote for him, actually.

How Trump created a "communism of pelf."

ROZSA: I'd now like to quote another Democratic president from over a century ago. Grover Cleveland warned against high tariffs. In 1894, he wrote that they are a "communism of pelf," and in 1887, he described excess tariffs as an "indefensible extortion" and a "culpable betrayal of American fairness and justice." Do you think those characterizations still hold up today? Why or why not?

McKILLEN: Well, I don't think they're entirely indefensible, but I think they always need to be targeted. And, of course, the interesting thing in comparison to Trump is that he worships William McKinley because McKinley initially supported tariffs. But, as I say, the thing about tariffs is that they need to be mutually agreed upon. What nations have discovered over time, of course, is that as the economy has become more and more global, it's become more and more important to cooperate in international economic treaties, rather than just to focus on nationalistic tariffs, which are widely viewed as often causing war, for example. Certainly high tariffs didn't help in the '30s. The economic pain brought by tariffs, as well as the bad settlement of World War I, helped to provoke German anger and lead to German fascism, of course.

So I think he had a point, but I'm not a proponent of total free trade either. I think American workers grew tired of free trade during the Cold War because, over the long run, they recognized that it had problems as well. So I think some tariffs are justified, but I think it's Bernie Sanders who has the best approach to this, in arguing that tariffs need democratic input and that they also need to be worked out in cooperation with other countries. One of the things Bernie Sanders suggested is that Americans should always focus on labor rights and that labor should have a role in any kind of tariff negotiations, so that workers' rights are protected, potentially in both countries if you're dealing with a bilateral trade agreement.

Ironically, one example of that was the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement that Trump signed in his first term, after initially resorting to high tariffs. That had a labor provision, a labor rights charter, and it had a system for monitoring as well, but it hasn't been adequately used ever since, and I'm not sure why. But it does strike me that what you really want to do is to have a set of trade negotiations where all significant actors are included and labor gets a voice, because I think it's important not just to talk about things from the perspective of business, but also from the perspective of labor and labor movements.

Now, the U.S. labor movement supported relative free trade in the immediate aftermath of World War II and during the Cold War, and it even became famous, belatedly, for working with the CIA to overthrow governments abroad that practiced protectionism or were more socialistic, as in the case of Salvador Allende in Chile. But after a while, they became disillusioned with that approach, and that started really in the aftermath of the Cold War, with the revolt against the World Trade Organization and some of those kinds of organizations in the '90s.

So again, and of course even Biden had tariffs, but I think they were more focused, and I think that's the key. And they need to be developed in cooperation with one's allies. That's the other irony of the Trump administration: he's been nastier in terms of tariffs with some of our closest allies, like Canada or Europe, rather than with world powers like China, or other countries that have historically been hostile to the United States.

So again, there's that issue of focused tariffs. And, you know, that's what McKinley eventually turned to, after Cleveland, who was very free trade, because he recognized that after the 1893 depression the tariffs weren't working, and so you needed overseas markets (and of course, that led to empire), and potentially you needed to work out various kinds of reciprocal trade agreements with other countries.

How Trump's tariffs fuel his corruption.

ROZSA: Returning to Grover Cleveland's earlier description of overly protectionist tariffs as a "communism of pelf": I would argue that Trump is engaging in corrupt activity through his tariff system because he privileges industries that are closer to the president and does not do so for industries that aren't as personally close to him; that, in a sense, he is creating a form of communism that is based on pelf, which is an archaic term for greed. Would you agree or disagree with this characterization? And if you agree with it, what are the ramifications for ordinary Americans economically of having a communism of pelf in this country?

McKILLEN: I think that's absolutely true with respect to Trump. I mean, his corruption is almost constant, and he's made billions off of being in the presidency. So I think that's true. I'm not sure that I agree with the idea that it's a communism. I think communism is a complex thing, and there have actually been democratic forms of communism as well as fanatical, dictatorial forms of communism. So I'm not sure I would put that term "communism" in there the same way Cleveland did. But I would say that I do think tariffs lend themselves to corruption by the president. And certainly that was true back in Grover Cleveland's period, when many of the corporations worked with the presidents directly to try to extend their own wealth, and then the president was doing the same thing.So yes, I think it's true that tariffs lend themselves to Trump's corruption, certainly, and they have in certain other periods as well.

ROZSA: And how does that hurt ordinary Americans?

McKILLEN: Well, it hurts them in the ways we've already talked about: it can artificially raise prices, and in fact those profits don't go back to building new factories or to raising the wages of workers. There are some interesting cartoons from that period, done by socialists or others, the left press, if you will, of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era. They always put tariffs on the side of big business and corruption, at the expense of workers, who were portrayed as becoming peasants again because all of their wages were being stolen by higher prices and by not getting paid enough. So there are some interesting cartoons about that from the Gilded Age.
news.summary:
Worker Pain: Trade wars have hiked consumer prices and destroyed American job security.
Allies Alienated: Aggressive protectionist tariffs have deeply damaged relations with Canada and Europe.
Corrupt System: New economic policies have fueled political corruption, creating a "communism of pelf."
Global Order Shattered: Protectionist strategies are dismantling generations of American diplomacy and international standing.
President Donald Trump's trade wars with Canada and Europe — who have traditionally been American allies — are more than merely "weird' (to quote economist Dr. Ed Gresser), although they are most certainly that. They have simultaneously done three things, all of them profoundly negative for both Americans and the rest of the world: First, they have raised prices for American workers while making their jobs less secure; second, they have hurt the United States' standing in the global community; and third, they have created a political culture rife with corruption.

news.title: An Iowa Judge Rejects Trump's Unconstitutional Attempt To Recover Damages for 'Fake News'
news.text:
On Wednesday, an Iowa judge dismissed a lawsuit in which President Donald Trump preposterously claimed that The Des Moines Register committed consumer fraud when it published poll results he did not like prior to the 2024 election. Those surprising results, which gave Kamala Harris, the Democratic presidential nominee, a lead in Iowa, turned out to be far off the mark. But according to Trump, that forecast was not only embarrassing but also illegal.

Trump's lawsuit, which he first filed in December 2024, alleged that the poll violated the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act, justifying damages to compensate him for "the extensive time and resources" required to "mitigate and counteract the harms" caused by the Register's reporting. That argument, if accepted, would expose journalists to the chilling threat of civil liability whenever someone claims they got a story wrong.

"At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability," Polk County District Court Judge Scott J. Beattie writes in his ruling against Trump. "After considering the parties' arguments, the Court must conclude that the protection is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed."

In addition to the Register, Trump sued pollster J. Ann Selzer, who conducted the survey at the heart of the case. "This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought," says Robert Corn-Revere, chief counsel at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), which represented Selzer. "The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of 'fake news.' That may work for him as a campaign slogan, but it is not a thing in the law."

The fraud exception to the First Amendment, Beattie notes, requires a provably false statement aimed at persuading someone to "part with money or property of value in reliance upon it." Trump's lawsuit, he concludes, fails to allege either element.

"A poll is simply an estimate," Beattie writes. "A poll reports responses from a sample of voters and includes a reported margin of error. It is based on a known methodology, and concerns an event that has not yet happened. Things of that nature are not the sort of things that can be said to be true or false in the manner required by the fraud exception."

Nor did Trump allege that he suffered an economic loss because he relied on statements by the Register or Selzer. "The constitutional fraud exception reaches lies told to obtain money or property," Beattie notes. "The misrepresentation must be made in the course of inducing the plaintiff to part with money, or property of value, in reliance upon it. None of that has been pleaded here."

Although Beattie says those failures would be enough to dispose of the case, he also addresses the specific elements required to prove a violation of the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act. He finds that Trump's allegations fail to satisfy those requirements and likewise do not meet the common-law tests for fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation. "Each cause of action the Plaintiffs invoke requires a connection between these parties that the Petition never pleads," he says.

Selzer's poll and the Register's reporting of its results "are fully protected political speech, and the Petition does not allege the elements that would place that speech within the fraud exception," Beattie concludes. "Independently, the Petition states no claim under Iowa law."

Beattie dismissed Trump's lawsuit with prejudice, meaning the president cannot try again. But despite the fundamental failures that Beattie identifies, Trump was able to tie Selzer and the Register up in court for nearly two years. "Such tactical claims are filed purely for the purpose of imposing punishing litigation costs on perceived opponents, not because they have any merit or stand any chance of success," FIRE says. "In other words, the lawsuit is the punishment."

Last year, Beattie notes, Iowa legislators approved the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, which "directs Iowa courts to resolve claims arising from the exercise of free speech on a matter of public concern at the earliest available stage." The law, which targets "strategic lawsuits against public participation" (SLAPPs), also requires unsuccessful plaintiffs in such cases to pay the defendants' legal expenses. But according to FIRE, Trump "purposefully filed" his latest complaint "just hours" before the anti-SLAPP law took effect.

In a Texas case based on similarly absurd fraud theories, Trump managed to extort $16 million from Paramount. Trump claimed CBS, which Paramount owned, had committed consumer fraud by editing a pre-election 60 Minutes interview with Harris in a way that made her seem slightly more cogent. That supposed fraud, he averred, had caused him "at least" $20 billion in damages.

After Trump filed the original version of that lawsuit in October 2024, CBS accurately described it as "completely without merit" and vowed to "vigorously defend against it." But Paramount's executives evidently thought $16 million was a small price to pay if it assuaged the president's wrath and avoided trouble with the Federal Communications Commission, which had launched a spurious "news distortion" investigation of the Harris interview and was mulling whether to approve Paramount's merger with Skydance Media.

As that settlement shows, frivolous lawsuits and presidential power are a dangerous combination. But unlike Paramount, the Register and Selzer were determined to resist Trump's attempt to treat "fake news" as a cause of action.

"This was never about 'consumer fraud,'" FIRE says. "Nor was it about winning in court. Trump's lawsuit was about intimidating perceived critics into silence by making them waste time and money on lawyers to defend perfectly legal speech."
news.summary: The dismissal of the president's lawsuit against The Des Moines Register is a victory for freedom of the press.
news.author: Jacob Sullum

news.title: New Hampshire Libertarian 'Vote GOP' Message Backs Assassinating Democrats
news.text: The Libertarian Party of New Hampshire is calling for political violence once again, this time targeting Democrats throughout the Granite State. The group, which has previously singled out Vice President Kamala Harris and a former state lawmaker, took aim Tuesday at Democrats in a since-deleted post on X. "We openly support the assassination of basically every elected Democrat in New Hampshire," the post read. "But if you don't have the balls to do that, you should probably GOP." Messages seeking comment from the organization were not immediately returned Thursday, but the state party later issued a clarification on Wednesday. "Some people seem to be misreading this," the group posted on X. "Few, if any, Americans actually have the balls to kill anyone, no matter how much tyranny they experience. We even went through Covid without a single assassination! The point is since no one wants to kill people, we have to vote." The unorthodox message had been quickly condemned by elected officials throughout New Hampshire, including Representative Chris Pappas. "Rhetoric calling for political assassination has no place in New Hampshire or our country — something we should all be able to agree on regardless of our political beliefs," Pappas said in a statement Wednesday. "We work out our differences through the democratic process where we engage in civil debate and seek common ground whenever possible." Pappas, a Democrat elected in 2019, urged his colleagues to condemn the threats while calling on social media platforms to enforce terms of use prohibiting threats of violence. "Our citizen-led government is a model for the nation, and we must ensure everyone can engage in democracy without fear of intimidation or violence," Pappas said. New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte characterized the post as "irresponsible and dangerous" while calling on the author to be prosecuted by authorities. "Violent rhetoric has no place in our politics, and threats like this should be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law," Ayotte told NHPR in a statement. The New Hampshire Attorney General's Office is aware of the post, but declined to comment further, NHPR reported. The state party, chaired by Jeremy Kauffman, lost its national affiliation in May after violating rules and ideals. The group's social media posts previously attracted the attention of law enforcement in 2024 after calling for Harris' assassination and claimed it was "perfectly permissible to kill" a former executive councilor for proposing a state income tax earlier this year, according to the outlet. Representative Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat who was elected last year, said Tuesday's post fell far short of embodying the ideals of liberty. "This is anti-American," Goodlander told WHDH. "It is downright dangerous. And no matter where you fall, which party you are in, where you fall on the ideological spectrum, this is something that should unite us as Americans in condemning.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: The Libertarian Party of New Hampshire is calling for political violence against Democrats throughout the Granite State.
news.author: Joshua Rhett Miller

news.title: Dispelling the myth that Republicans are defecting from Trump
news.text:
Just like the ever-elusive yet somehow continual sightings of Bigfoot and the Loch Ness Monster, it seems that every so often there are fanciful whispers of Republican lawmakers en masse breaking away from President Donald Trump.

When it comes to Trump’s relationship with Republicans, though, the actual explanation is far less sensational than many headlines would have us believe. All you really have to do is look at the poll numbers to understand why certain candidates take certain positions — or, in the case of some Republicans, inch away from Trump.

In the past, and out of fear, most Republicans nibbled around the edges when trying to show their independence from Trump.

With just a couple of weeks to go until early voting starts in many states, a few vulnerable Republicans are taking calculated risks in breaking with Trump on issues they sense their constituents will respond to. In other words, it is better to win and say sorry than to be a loyal foot soldier and lose.

In the past, and out of fear, most Republicans nibbled around the edges when trying to show their independence from Trump, but last week Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., took a big public swipe at Trump, running a television ad in which she addressed the president straight to camera:

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

In Michigan, Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, distanced himself from Trump on the war with Iran in a new ad where he says, “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly.”

It is very likely that these two candidates are relying on Trump’s transactional nature and the possibility that he might even respect them for stepping out of line — as long as they win. For Salazar, this was a good bet. While Trump disagreed with her, when asked if he still supported her after he saw the ad, Trump said, “I do and I have.”

Because Michigan is a possible pickup seat for Republicans, it is also likely that Trump will stay quiet on Rogers. But there should be little doubt that should these candidates win, not only would Trump take credit for it, he would also demand full obedience and loyalty, lest they feel the full wrath of Trump.

Some candidates are trying to move away from Trump on the sly — a decidedly riskier move, much more likely to arouse the ire of Trump than earn his respect. Rep. Bryon Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in Florida, is in a dead heat with his Democratic challenger, according to recent public polling. Donalds scrubbed his website of almost all mentions of Trump, including a now-deleted section titled “Enact the Trump Agenda.” Unlike Salazar or Rogers, Donalds’ is a very dicey move.

For one, taking down a Trump endorsement goes directly to the president’s well-documented ego. Second, Trump doesn’t respect cowards. If you’re going to disagree with him, do it straight on like Salazar and Rogers, not by trying to slip under the radar hoping that Trump is too distracted by other news, and that no one notices.

Trump doesn’t respect cowards. If you’re going to disagree with him, do it straight on. 

There is one Republican who has been able to thread the needle quite well. Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, having won re-election in 2024 in a district that went for Vice President Kamala Harris 49.9% to 49.3%, is in one of the most competitive races in the country. Lawler has used his disagreements with the president strategically, while not completely running away from him.

In essence, Lawler has mastered the Trump weave. While he hosted a rally with Trump in May, he also ran a political ad that included him saying he took on the policial right, with a clip of Trump calling him a “pain in the ass” over fighting for the SALT, or state and local tax, deduction. Then, a couple of weeks after speaking at the Republican midterm convention, aka "Trumpapalooza," Lawler ran an attack ad against his opponent, Cait Conley, on her support for data centers.

So yes, some Republicans are making calculated decisions to edge away from Trump. But the majority of them are sticking with the president. That’s because they know they need his voters to win, and they are afraid of moving against him because they will be up for re-election 18 months from now and are understandably afraid of retribution in a primary.

The Republican Party isn’t leaving Trump. That doesn’t mean there aren’t some rare exceptions of course — just this past week Sen. John Curtis of Utah went where no Republican has gone before, targeting a member of the Trump family by calling for an investigation of both Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden. Then again, Curtis isn’t up for re-election until 2030.
news.author: Laura Barrón-López

news.title: How a Russian Attack on the Midterms Deepfaked Mother Jones
news.text:
As MS NOW and The New York Times have each reported, in the past two weeks, a Russian disinformation network disinformation analysts have dubbed Storm-1679 or Matryoshka (the Russian word for those iconic nesting dolls) has begun to inject false election-related material into US social media.

Most notably, its phony posts include purported videos of Hollywood celebrities disparaging Democrats and urging votes for Republican candidates. In one, actor Sarah Jessica Parker appears to say, “When I hear about Democrats, I immediately think of corrupt Nazi whores. If you love America, never vote for Democrats.” The video was branded with a CNN logo and contained the hashtag #AllDemocratsAreCriminals. Other deepfakes in this campaign have used doctored footage of Christopher Lloyd, Ed Begley Jr., and Julia Roberts.

This latest Matryoshka operation was first identified by @antibot4navalny, a small group of anonymous activists who track Russian influence operations. This outfit has revealed that Matryoshka has been disseminating on social media fake CNN reports with false allegations about Democratic senatorial candidates. One targeting James Talarico of Texas declares he “despises Hasidic Jews because their faith does not allow children to change their gender.”

The @antibot4navalny trackers have spotted dozens of false reports spewed out by Matryoshka that are created to look as if they come from The New York Times, The Washington Post, NPR, Politico, PBS, ABC News, NBC News, CBS News, MS NOW, and other major American media outlets. Many stick to the celebrity-says-Democrats-are-horrible theme. Others spread false reports about corruption at US media outlets, and some pretend to be news reports showing that stories about Russian disinformation are phony. 

This is not Matryoshka’s first rodeo. In my new book, How Russia Won: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and the Fight for America, I covered the network’s role in the massive Russian disinformation operation that targeted the 2024 presidential campaign to tarnish Democratic nominee Kamala Harris and boost Trump. I wrote:

The Matryoshka operation produced numerous social media posts and videos falsely branded as reports from major news outlets (such as Fox News, BBC, and CNN), government agencies, and research outfits. It spewed a barrage of disinformation: Harris had an abortion when she was seventeen (Fox News). She was exhibiting early--onset Alzheimer’s (USA Today). Her grandfather was a communist (BBC). Her family was connected to Pfizer and Big Pharma (Bellingcat). It also disseminated a report supposedly from USA Today claiming Ukrainian refugees were smuggling fentanyl into the United States, and it generated material to stoke fears of civil war in the United States, postelection violence, and a full--scale conflict between the United States and Russia that could result in nuclear catastrophe.

In the first three months of 2025, Matryoshka tried to undercut Western support for Ukraine by putting out false news reports depicting Kyiv as corrupt and belligerent and claiming Europe was being dragged into World War III. These messages, according to disinformation researchers, did not gain much traction. 

But during one of Elon Musk’s tirades against the US Agency for International Development, which he was then trying to abolish, he shared with his 216 million followers on X a clip from E! News reporting that the agency had paid millions to celebrities to travel to Ukraine. The roster included Angelina Jolie ($20 million), Orlando Bloom ($8 million), Sean Penn ($5 million), and Ben Stiller ($4 million). Donald Trump Jr. reposted the video as well; it quickly drew more than 11 million views. That video was a Matryoshka fake.

After Mother Jones was alerted by @antibot4navalny, a lawyer for Mother Jones contacted X to register a complaint about the phony video with the implausible claim the DNC had paid more than one-quarter of a billion dollars to CNN’s chief. “Thanks for bringing this to our attention,” X responded. “We’ve removed the reported post(s) for a violation of X Rules and specifically our trademark policy.” As of now, Matryoshka’s current operation does not seem to have achieved great reach on X, Bluesky, or other social media platforms. But in 2024, the Russian disinformation campaign placed false anti-Democrats messages in the feeds of millions of Americans. One bogus allegation—Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, the Democratic vice presidential candidate, had inappropriately touched an exchange student when he was a high school teacher—did go viral and was amplified by Jack Posobiec, the promoter of Pizzagate and a MAGA provocateur who had been working with the Republican Party, and Candace Owens, a popular right-wing influencer. Matryoshka’s new operation aimed at the midterms may not yet have produced viral content, but it signals that Putin is at it again. He has mounted disinformation and influence operations in every national US election since 2016 (as my book chronicles)—to sow discord and to help Trump. This time, Russian disinformation warfare is occurring with the United States less able to defend against this threat. The Trump administration has shuttered the units at the FBI, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the State Department that once tracked Russian disinformation (and disinformation from other foreign adversaries) and sought to counter it.

With Trump leaving the door wide open (purposefully?), Matryoshka and other Russian disinformation ops will have a clear shot at influencing the midterm elections—to help Republican candidates and, perhaps more important, exacerbate any chaos or conflict that might arise. This could be a far bigger and more consequential operation than a fake Robert De Niro, Charlize Theron, or Cher post.

news.title: California Governor Newsom says Trump presidency 'as we know it' ends in November
news.text: NEW YORK: California Governor Gavin Newsom has a prediction for November: Democrats retake the House, and Donald Trump's presidency "as we know it" is over."We're going to take back the House of Representatives. It's a day of reckoning, a new day coming," Newsom told AFP and two other outlets after a UN climate summit in New York."Trump's presidency, as we know it, ends in November," said the 58-year-old outgoing Democratic leader of the nation's most populous state, widely seen as a leading contender for his party's 2028 presidential nomination.Newsom, who spoke Wednesday, did not give details on how he thinks a Democratic win would in essence end the Trump presidency.But if Trump's Republicans lose control of one or both houses of Congress, Democrats can in fact curb the president’s expansive agenda -- though the executive still wields considerable power.Newsom also insisted climate was winning politics -- if framed not as a "green" issue but as one tied to everything from grocery prices to home insurance to national security."People say 'why the hell are you talking about that, you should be talking about the kitchen table,' I said 'I am!'"He pointed to the price of beef and coffee, and the challenges of insuring a home or getting a mortgage amid growing climate risks from more extreme wildfires to coastal erosion supercharged by El Nino..Trump promises each American $5,000 if Republicans keep Congress in midterms.California a green pioneerOther politicians shy away from the subject, he said, "because they don't know how to talk about it, and those that have talked about in the past have been accused of being soft, weak, effete, green, hyperbolic."He conceded that "some of our language did get a little apocalyptic." The key, he said, is hammering home that "it's not about electric power; it's about economic power. It's about statecraft."At the summit, he pitched California as proof that climate action and growth go hand in hand, saying the state -- the world's fourth-largest economy, whose GDP has grown 40 percent since 2019 -- had run on 100 percent clean energy for at least part of the day on 90 percent of days this year.His administration has battled Trump and congressional Republicans over efforts to undo California's green rules -- from scrapping its planned phase-out of gasoline cars to paying companies to abandon offshore wind projects."Donald Trump wants to recreate the 19th century," said Newsom. "He's doubling down on stupid. He's putting America in reverse.""Whoever the nominee is of the Democratic Party is going to be the next president of the United States," he said.Any of the Democratic hopefuls, he added, would be "exponentially better than a Rubio or Vance that have countenanced this corruption, this grift, this graft, this destruction of truth and trust and institutions," referring to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance.They are seen as the likely Republican front-runners, though neither has declared..Trump promises to campaign for Republicans, says they have 'winning' midterm message.'Old rules don't apply'Left-wing Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made waves this week when she told The New York Times she was weighing a run, musing about whether a Latina could win in a country that rejected female nominees in 2016 and 2024.AOC, Newsom and Jon Ossoff, a charismatic Jewish senator from Georgia, are among the favorites on betting markets."She absolutely could become the nominee of the party. That's my assessment of electability. This notion that a woman can't win is insulting," Newsom said, blaming "punditry" for perpetuating the trope."I'm done with people talking like that. Or that if you're from California or you're Jewish or you're old or you're too young -- give me a damn break. Our politics is completely scrambled post-Trump. The old rules, they do not apply."Though he called Ocasio-Cortez a "generational talent," he pointedly did not rule out running against her -- having told CNN emphatically last week that he would not challenge Kamala Harris, the 2024 nominee, with whom he shares a history in California that predates politics."It's a different framework," he said. "I don't have a relationship that goes back to before we were both in politics. I don't have a relationship in the context of our base overlaying in remarkable ways.Whether Newsom runs, he said, depends on whether he can "look them and you in the eye and say I have something unique they don't... voice, experience, perspective, capacity that is unique and distinctive.".US midterm polls: Democrats and Republicans draw battle lines for November after primaries.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Taylor Swift 'takes action' against Trump after he tried to use her for concerning immigration post
news.text:
Taylor Swift appears to have put her foot down after Donald Trump once again used her music in a political post.

Trump and his team are known for landing themselves in hot water for using artists' music seemingly without their permission, Swift included.

Last year, the president caused uproar with the 'Bad Blood' hitmaker's fans after he used her song 'The Fate of Ophelia' in a TikTok video. In the clip, the social media team edited the lyrics to the 'Fate of America'.

Swifties quickly jumped into action and called on the singer to 'sue' Trump.

"Oh hell no, they didn’t do this to Taylor! As a Swiftie, I am sooo mad and hope she goes for them," one person raged at the time.

It appears as if the audio has since been removed from the clip - potentially at Swift's team's insistence - but that didn't stop Trump using another of her songs in a similar manner.

On the official 'team Trump' Instagram page, they bragged that zero so-called 'illegals' have crossed the border in over 16 months.

Initially, they had added Swift's 'Father Figure' over the picture, but it looks like the singer's team have quietly had it removed. The clip now has no audio.

It's somewhat surprising that Trump tries to use Swift's music because it's safe to say that the POTUS hasn't had the nicest things to say about the record-breaking artist.

What Donald Trump has said about Taylor Swift previously

Once the businessman-turned-politician was complimentary about the singer, but his tune quickly changed after she endorsed Democratic candidates. In 2024, Swift endorsed Kamala Harris, and four years earlier she'd endorsed Joe Biden.

After she endorsed Harris, Trump shared a post that said he 'hates' her. Then, in 2025, he said that Swift was no longer 'hot'. He said online in May last year: "Has anyone noticed that, since I said 'I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,' she’s no longer 'HOT?'"

Swift has been arguably more diplomatic when it comes to her public condemnation of the POTUS, but it's quite clear she isn't in favor of him and his party.

Trump has used other artists' music as well

In December 2025, Trump's team used Sabrina Carpenter's son 'Juno' in one of its online posts about ICE, which she quickly spoke out about.

"This video is evil and disgusting. Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda," Carpenter said at the time.

And in June this year, Ariana Grande hit out at Trump for using her song 'Bye' in a social media video about deportations.

She said: "Please do not use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense."

The White House hit back: "What's actually barbaric, inhumane, and heinous are the criminal illegal ‌aliens ⁠who have injured and murdered innocent American citizens."

Rihanna, Neil Young, ABBA, Céline Dion, and The White Stripes have also hit out at Trump for using their music, some of whom even threatened legal action.
news.summary: Donald Trump has previously used Taylor Swift's music without her permission
news.author: Niamh Shackleton

news.title: Abdul El Sayed Targeted At Town Hall Over Response To Iran Leader's Death
news.text: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate for Michigan, was challenged during a town hall over why he did not unequivocally condemn the Iranian regime and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Iman Dashti, who identified himself as Persian, told El-Sayed during a town hall at the University of Michigan that his family had been persecuted by the regime in Tehran. Dashti said he was dismayed when leaked audio emerged in which El Sayed did not want to comment on the death of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei following U.S. strikes on Iran because “there are a lot of people in Dearborn who are sad today.” “That silence had a gaping hole in our community," said Dashti as he asked El-Sayed whether “you stand unequivocally against the IRGC?” El-Sayed appeared to evade a direct criticism of the late Ayatollah, replying, “I will always stand for and with democratic movements" but that he opposed U.S. involvement in regime change. Mike Rogers, his Republican rival for the Senate, criticized El-Sayed's reply, posting on X: "Abdul El-Sayed is looking a young man in the eyes and can’t even condemn a terrorist dictator murdering thousands of his own people. Pathetic." Newsweek has contacted El-Sayed's office for comment. Where Did The Exchange Take Place? The tense exchange took place at the Michigan Theater in Ann Arbor during a University of Michigan town hall event on Wednesday titled "Students vs. Billionaires." It was part of a statewide campus tour organized by More Perfect University to engage voters across the state ahead of November's mid-term elections. When asked if he regretted not denouncing the IRGC, El-Sayed criticized military intervention, telling the crowd that "for too long and too often, when we think about our role in the world, we have turned ourselves into the world's policeman." "I will always stand for and with democratic movements, always," El-Sayed said before taking a swipe at the Trump administration's actions, adding, "I also don't believe that we were in the right to go to war to topple the government of Iran." He received some applause for his comments, but they prompted criticism among social media users. The X account of Democrats for Mike Rogers posted: "Abdul can’t condemn Hamas, the IRGC, the Houthis, or the enemies of America. We deserve better." News anchor Harris Faulkner posted on X next to the clip, "you’ll notice Michigan candidate for US Senate Abdul EL-Sayed never condemned the IRGC. Why not?" El Sayed vs. Rogers: What latest polls say Ahead of the mid-term elections on November 3, the latest polling shows a very tight race in Michigan, with El-Sayed slightly ahead in the race for the Senate seat vacated by Democratic incumbent Gary Peters, who will not seek re-election. The pair is competing in one of seven Senate races that the election handicapper Cook Political Report has called a “toss-up.” A Pollsmax average put the Democrat El-Sayed at 46.4 percent as of Thursday. 1.6 percentage points ahead of Republican Mike Rogers' 44.8 percent. A poll released Monday by the Suffolk University Political Research Center gave El-Sayed a 7-point lead over Rogers, with four other candidates combined for 3 percent. Some 8 percent of voters were undecided. Meanwhile, Emerson College polling between September 12 and September 14, which put El-Sayed two percentage points ahead of his GOP rival, highlighted how education shapes attitudes towards the Democrat. Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, said his firm's survey found that voters without a four-year degree favor Rogers, 48 percent to 45 percent, while college graduates backed the Democrat El-Sayed, 53 percent to 4 percent. Why the Michigan Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterms The GOP has a 53-47 majority in the U.S. Senate, including two independents who caucus with Democrats, and needs a net gain of four seats to take control of the upper house. The Cook Political Report considers seven Senate contests as toss-ups, with Michigan among them. The others are Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire and Ohio. Five of the seven seats are held by Republicans and two by Democrats. news.title: Trump's lawsuit against pollster, newspaper dismissed in Iowa
news.text:
Sept. 24 (UPI) -- An Iowa judge dismissed President Donald Trump's lawsuit alleging fraud on the part of pollster J. Ann Selzer and The Des Moines Register.

Iowa District Court Judge Scott J. Beattie ruled Wednesday that the pollster and newspaper did not violate state consumer fraud laws by publishing a poll days before the 2024 election that showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris leading Trump by 3 percentage points in the state, The Hill and The New York Times reported.

Trump went on to win the state by 14 points.

"At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability," Beattie wrote in the ruling.

"After considering the parties' arguments, the Court must conclude that the protection is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed," he wrote.

Beattie dismissed the case with prejudice, which means the lawsuit cannot be refiled by Trump's team.

The suit, which also named Selzer & Company, Selzer's polling firm, and Gannett, the Register's parent company, as defendants, alleged that publishing the poll amounted to "brazen election interference" and violated the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act.

Bob Corn-Revere, a lawyer for the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, which is representing Selzer, praised the ruling.

"We're pleased that the court recognized what we've said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought," Corn-Revere told The New York Times. "The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of 'fake news.'"

Seltzer also welcomed the ruling in a statement provided to The Hill.

"Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome," she said. "What we can guarantee is that we will follow the data wherever it leads, even when the results are uncomfortable or unexpected. I am grateful that Judge Beattie's ruling recognizes these principles and reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference."

Trump's legal team did not immediately respond to the ruling.
news.summary: An Iowa judge dismissed President Donald Trump's lawsuit alleging fraud on the part of pollster J. Ann Selzer and The Des Moines Register.

news.title: CNN, MS NOW And Politico Denied Access To White House Despite Judge's Order
news.text:
WASHINGTON, Sept 24 (Reuters) - CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists were barred from the White House on Thursday, just hours after a federal judge deemed US President Donald Trump‘s ban of the three news outlets likely unconstitutional and ordered their access immediately restored.

The news organizations responded by requesting an immediate hearing before US District Judge Tim Kelly, whose ruling overnight ordered a halt to the ban for 14 days in a major setback for Trump. It is the latest in a series of confrontations over press freedom that have played out over the past week in the courtroom and White House grounds.

Kelly found that the revocation of the White House credentials of the journalists “likely violated their constitutional due process rights.”

The judge, who Trump appointed in 2017 during his first presidential term, also raised doubts about the US Department of Justice’s national security arguments for justifying the ban, noting that Trump himself had said the action was due to what the president alleged was false or negative coverage.

Just hours after the ruling, however, the outlets still had not gained access to the White House. Whether that was due to intentional defiance of Kelly’s order or a matter of confusion within the White House security staff and systems remained unclear.

Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Politico reporter’s credentials were confiscated, Politico said, while an MS NOW reporter said she was blocked from the White House. CNN said some of its staff members were denied entry onto the grounds.

Trump announced the ban last Friday on his social media platform, saying those news organizations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” Trump framed their reporting as a threat to US national security.

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration on Monday, saying the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organizations, including Reuters, later filed a legal brief supporting the three news outlets.

National security concerns 

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and stop enforcing the ban for two weeks. The judge rejected the administration’s stated national security concerns.

“The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” Kelly wrote.

In a filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security with their coverage, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump’s White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican midterm convention.

Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the three outlets, welcomed the judge’s decision in a statement, saying: “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”

In the wake of Trump’s ban, other members of the White House press pool of reporters who share resources to follow the US president’s movements have refused to record or disseminate his events until access is restored for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, acting in solidarity with their fellow journalists.

This occurred as Trump spoke at the United Nations and hosts Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington this week, including events at the White House on Thursday.

There were no TV pool cameras set up for Xi’s arrival on the White House’s South Lawn Thursday morning, and FOX News, MS NOW and CNN did not air the two leaders’ arrival ceremony live.

Tensions with the press 

Although other presidential administrations have battled with the press, Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented. Upending decades of tradition, his White House had denied basic access to many major news organizations, launched personal attacks on journalists and filed multiple lawsuits against news organizations.

Kelly’s ruling came a day after Trump experienced another legal setback.

On Wednesday, an Iowa judge dismissed Trump’s 2024 lawsuit against the Des Moines Register newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer. Trump sued the Register, its parent company Gannett and Selzer over a poll published ahead of the November 2024 US election that showed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris leading him in Iowa. Trump accused the newspaper and its longtime pollster of fraudulently misleading readers.

In his ruling Wednesday, Iowa District Judge Scott Beattie said the poll was legally protected speech.

(Reporting by Susan Heavey in Washington and Helen Coster in New York; additional reporting by Katharine Jackson, Gram Slattery, Trevor Hunicutt and Jack Queen; Editing by Paul Thomasch, Doina Chiacu and Will Dunham)
